content:
Thick slices are often preferred instead of thin slices. This helps to
increase signal to noise ratio and to limit the examination time by
reducing the number of slices. However, this may result in partial
volume effects. These are caused by high density tissues (such as a
bone) or objects (such as pacemakers) projecting only partly into the
slice plane. One such well-known artifact is the so-called Hounsfield
bar between the petrous bones. Other regions of the skull are also
problematic with regard to partial volume effects which are visible as
dark streaks. Additional correction and / or special parameter settings
(head modes) help to minimize these effects.
◾To avoid partial volume effects, use thinner slices.
When X-ray beams pass through tissue, the average energy of the
radiation spectrum is shifted towards higher energy. This is known as
beam hardening. It depends on the material density and thickness of
the tissue through which the X-ray beam passes.
For body parts similar in density to water, for example, soft tissue, the
effect on the CT image can be compensated. In areas of high density
such as hips, shoulders or lower skull, hypodense streaks and areas
with reduced CT values can be seen. Along the sides of the upper part
of the skull, the so-called “cupping effect” can be seen as a
brightening of the CT values. The cupping effect also occurs in rare
cases such as infant skull tomograms, due to residual extra focal
radiation.
Additional corrections and/or special kernel parameter settings (head
modes) help to minimize these effects. Yet, they cannot fully
eliminate them.
Metal objects such as tooth fillings, surgical clips, jewelry, hair clips,
belts or hip prostheses, and so on, can cause extreme forms of beam
hardening artifacts. Depending on density and size, they can lead to
total absorption of the radiation. This results in corresponding strong
black or white streaks or star-shaped artifacts.
Movement of organs in the slice or displacement of the entire slice
during scanning likewise causes bright and dark artifacts. These are
usually seen as streaks or in areas of low density. To reduce motion
artifacts use the automatic patient instructions (API) function for
breathing and swallowing commands.

System related artifacts
System related artifacts may be due to the following:
◾Uncalibrated system
◾Detector deviations
If the CT system is not properly setup (for example, no check-up
performed) CT scale displacements and inhomogeneities can result.
This may result just after switching on the unit, during warm-up to
operational temperature (calibration), or due to an extended length
of service of the X-ray tube. The same applies to defects in the
measurement system.
The daily quality checkup usually detects and reports such
discrepancies. Additional calibrations may also be necessary if large
changes in temperature occur in the room.
CAUTION
When you restart the system, the detector has not yet reached
operating temperature!
Wrong diagnosis due to image artifacts.
◆Calibrate the system as part of the checkup. Repeat
calibration if ring artifacts occur.
Other system defects or calibration deviations cause streaks or
(partial) rings to appear in the CT image.

content:
In CT systems with a rotating combined tube-detector system even
minimal deviations of individual detector channels from the original
calibration level may lead to rings or partial ring artifact structures in
the CT image. The closer such channels lie to the detector center, the
greater are these effects.
In an extreme case, rings may appear concentrated as a blurred spot
in the center of the scan field (the scan field center appears at the
image center if the Center X and Y image parameters are both zero).
Such rings are easily recognizable, but a blurred spot in the center of
the scan field might lead to inaccurate diagnoses.
Scan repetition due to image artifacts
Measurement related or system related artifacts cannot always be
excluded. Therefore the scan should be repeated if a tomographic
structure appears questionable. This should be done after slightly
shifting the patient’s position within the slice, for example, by
changing vertical position of the table by more than 5 mm. The result
can be used to exclude system-dependent long-term or temporary
equipment faults as the artifact cause.
CAUTION
Artifacts affecting the diagnosis are evident or suspected in a
patient image, or the patient may have moved during scanning!
Improper diagnosis possible.
◆Scanning must, under all circumstances, be repeated with a
slight shift in patient position.
Persisting object related artifacts can be considered measurement-
related with a high probability. They should be recognizable as such
by an experienced radiologist.

content:
Scan protocols
A scan protocol pre-defines examination steps. Scan protocols are the
building blocks to set up the examination procedure. Siemens
Healthineers provides you with a large set of scan protocols that
cover most of your routine CT examinations. You can also create your
own scan protocols.
◾You can create, edit, or delete scan protocols using Scan Protocol
Assistant.
◾During patient registration, you can select a scan protocol from the
Study list in the Patient Registration dialog box.
◾At any time before an exam is closed, you can modify the
examination procedure by selecting scan protocols in Patient
Model Dialog.

Siemens scan protocols provide an optimized set of default
parameters balancing image quality, scan time, and patient dose.
They are defined to be applied directly to your examination after
minor adaptions of, for example, the language of the Automatic
Patient Instructions. Special clinical conditions and applications
may require the adaption of the default recommendations. As
the final diagnosis is the sole responsibility of the user, the user
always has to make sure that the chosen scan protocol meets the
requirements of the examination.
Creating custom scan protocols
You can create a custom scan protocol based on either a Siemens
default protocol or an existing custom protocol. When you modify a
Siemens default protocol, the modified protocol becomes a custom
protocol. You can create a custom scan protocol in the following
ways:
◾Load a base protocol into Chronicle. Then, you can manipulate
Chronicle, for example by adding/deleting exam steps or changing
exam parameters. Finally, select Edit > Save Scan Protocol to save
Chronicle in a new scan protocol.
◾Use Scan Protocol Assistant to edit a scan protocol.

1 Select Edit > Delete Scan Protocol from the main menu.
2 In the Delete Scan Protocol window, double-click the folder of a
protocol group. For example, abdomen protocols can be found in
the MIAbdomen folder.
3 Select the protocols you want to delete.
4 Click Delete.

◾You can select multiple protocols to be deleted.
◾You need to enter a password to delete a scan protocol, if the
password is set in Configuration > Application in Local
Service.
Average CT
The CT standard spiral mode acquires only a subset of all patient
based movements (caused by breathing, heart beat) during an
examination. Compared to the radiotherapy data, CT data has no
patient or organ movements.
Average CT mode allows you to acquire a CT volume that shows
organ motion as a blurred image. The system provides a spiral mode
with special parameters. With the very low pitch factor, the system
can cover the full breathing cycle with one blurry image. This mode is
only possible with special scan protocols marked with the suffix
“Avg”.

The average CT mode helps the radio-oncologists in radiotherapy
treatment planning to visualize the tumor excursion for a better
understanding of the target volume. With average CT, you can
identify structures, such as lung lesions, during breathing.
On the Scan subtask card, the Average CT option is available. When
using an average CT scan protocol, the option is automatically
selected.
Only certain slice thicknesses are available for average CT. Collimation
and rotation time cannot be changed. The Series Description is
extended by the suffix “AvgCT”.
CAUTION

Wrong diagnosis.
◆The image generated by the Average CT mode shall not be
used in normal CT diagnosis because of the possible artifacts
and low resolution.

tube voltage of 80 kV and the minimum tube current is used
for average CT. By default, CARE Dose4D is switched off in an
average CT scan protocol.

indicate clearly that images generated in this mode should not
be used for the purpose of CT diagnosis.

Patient positioning safety
If the system is operated correctly and the patient is correctly
positioned, there is very little risk of injury to the patient or
personnel.
The patient must be positioned in such a way that he or she cannot
collide with or be injured by table top movements or the tilting
movement of the gantry.
◾Immobilize the arms of the patient with the straps supplied to rule
out collisions and injury to the hands under the table top.
◾Special caution is required with obese, unconscious, apathetic,
unresponsive, or pediatric patients. With obese patients, make sure
that no collision occurs.
CAUTION
Incorrect patient positioning!
Injury to the patient by moving parts.
◆Make sure that neither the patient’s clothing nor hair can get
caught in mechanical parts.
◆Make sure that infusion lines and respiration tubes, catheters
and ECG cables cannot get caught in the space between the
table top and the side parts. These components must not be
put under tensile stress in any other way.
◆Make sure that patient bedding cannot get caught by moving
parts of the patient table.
◆Use positioning aids as described.
Before you start the examination convince yourself that the patient is
not endangered either by the movement of the table or by the tilt of
the gantry.

Patient instructions
If the patient must hold his or her breath during CT acquisitions,
please ensure he or she is instructed how to prior to examination.
This especially applies to examinations of the thorax and abdomen.
However, the slight movement that respiration inevitably causes, can
also lead to artifacts in other regions.
◾Explain to the patient before the examination how he or she
should breathe.

a relatively long time.
◾Use the intercom system to give the patient breathing instructions.

Routine examination
A CT examination consists of the following steps:
◾Preparing an examination
– Patient registration
– Patient positioning
◾Loading a scan protocol
A scan protocol pre-defines exam steps. After you click the Exam
button in the Patient Registration dialog box. Patient Model
Dialog appears automatically for you to select a scan protocol. The
scan protocol is then loaded into the Examination task card.
◾Scanning a patient
– Acquiring a topogram
– Acquiring tomograms
◾Reconstructing images
A CT scan collects the image raw data. From the raw data, it is
possible to reconstruct several sets of diagnostic images with
different recon parameters. Image reconstruction is done in recon
jobs. Every scan comes with at least one default recon job. if
necessary, you can create additional recon jobs to reconstruct
more images.
◾Evaluating images
◾Documenting exam results

Suspending a topo scan
✓A topo scan is in progress.
◆Do any of the following:
◾Click Suspend.
◾Press Suspend on CT control box.
The topo scan is stopped. Part of the topogram remains in the topo
segment.

If you suspend a topo scan during the scan start delay, the scan is
unloaded.
Linking two topo scans
When you link two topo scans together, you can acquire a pair of
topograms in different views (anterior-posterior view/lateral view) or
different directions (head to feet/feet to head) with the same scan
range. This helps you to plan the scan range or pre-plan the recon
range for the following tomo scan more accurately, especially for
body regions that are smaller than the body’s contour, such as the
heart or spine disc. All Siemens default cardio and SpineSeq scan
protocols are provided with two linked topo scans.
✓There is a topo scan entry in Chronicle.
1 Insert a new topo scan entry immediately after the existing one.
2 Select the newly-created topo scan entry.
3 Select the Attach to previous Topogram check box on the
Routine sub-task card.

A dual topo indicator (
) is displayed, which indicates that the
two topo scans are linked. The current topo scan becomes the
secondary topo scan and the previous topo scan becomes the
primary topo scan.
The following parameter settings of the secondary topo scan are
automatically adapted to the primary topo scan:
◾Topogram length: same as the primary topo scan. You can
change the topogram length, if required. Once it has been
changed manually, it will no longer automatically replicate the
topogram length from the primary topo scan.
◾Tube position: different from the primary topo scan. For
example, if the tube position of the primary topo scan is Top or
Bottom, the tube position of the secondary topo scan is
automatically updated to Lateral. However, you can change the
tube position, if required.
◾Direction: opposite to the primary topo scan. You can change
the direction, if required.

◾To unlink two topo scans, clear the Attach to previous
Topogram check box on the Routine sub-task card of the
secondary topo scan.
◾If you remove the primary topo scan entry from Chronicle, the
linked secondary topo scan entry will be removed as well.
Planning an exam range
The exam range should be planned on a topogram to cover the
desired anatomic region for diagnosis. First of all, you can zoom or
pan the topogram for a better view. Several ways help you to define a
range efficiently.

Slice width
The slice width is the thickness of the reconstructed tomographic
images. It determines the image definition (spatial resolution). As a
rule, the slice width should correspond to the smallest anatomic
structure to be displayed.
A thicker slice reduces the number of images to be reconstructed and
may speed up an examination, but results in poorer image definition.
A thinner slice produces good image definition for better separation
of neighboring structures, for example, in the inner ear.
On the Recon sub-task card, you can select the slice width of a recon
job in the Slice list. This recon slice is no thinner than the scan slice
defined in the scan collimation.
Recon increment
The recon increment defines the distance between recon images.
If the increment is smaller than the slice width, the images are
reconstructed with overlaps. This improves the image quality for 3D
post-processing. If the increment is larger than the slice width, the
images are reconstructed with gaps in between.
Window
Window values (window width and window center) define the
brightness and contrast of recon images, based on organ-specific CT
values. Appropriate window values produce images with an
optimized appearance for a particular organ.
On the Recon sub-task card, you can choose the organ-specific
window values in the Window list.

Kernel
On the Recon sub-task card, kernels are selected in the Kernel list,
for example, B90s. A kernel is a recon parameter affecting image
sharpness and noise.
Each kernel's name starts with a capitalized letter representing the
body region or a special application. B stands for body; H stands for
head; U stands for Ultra High Resolution; C stands for child head; S
stands for a special application (for example, syngo Osteo CT).
The image sharpness is defined by the number in the kernel's name.
The higher the number, the sharper the image.

60-70
High resolution
80-90
Iterative metal artifact reduction
Metal objects, such as metal implants or metal markers, can cause
beam hardening artifacts. Depending on density and size, these metal
objects can lead to a total absorption of radiation resulting in strong
black or white streaks or star-shaped artifacts. Such artifacts can be
reduced by the iterative Metal Artifact Reduction (iMAR) algorithm.
iMAR can be used in conjunction with several other recon options:
◾iMAR works for both axial and 3D recon.
◾iMAR works with extended FoV.
◾iMAR works with an Iterative Reconstruction method.

The images reconstructed with iMAR may not be exactly the
same as the images reconstructed using a conventional method.
Therefore, it is recommended to use both reconstruction
methods.

content:
Iterative reconstruction
Depending on your scanner type and license, one of the following
iterative reconstruction methods is available.
◾IRIS
◾SAFIRE
Iterative Reconstruction in Image Space (IRIS) an image-based
iterative reconstruction method using a special algorithm. Compared
with the common reconstruction method based on the same image
raw data, the reconstruction with the IRIS algorithm produces images
with less noise and enhanced image sharpness.
To activate IRIS, click the IRIS check box on the Recon sub-task card.
When a recon job is set up to use IRIS, the recon job number is
marked in blue.
When you select the IRIS check box, the Kernel list on the Recon sub-
task card changes to the Algorithm list. An algorithm's name starts
with the character I or J, for example, I30s or J40. Algorithm I
corresponds to kernel B. Algorithm J corresponds to kernel H.

◾Use of IRIS requires a license.
◾IRIS cannot work with extended CT scale.
◾Do not use IRIS images for evaluation with the syngo Osteo or
CaScoring applications.
Sinogram Affirmed Iterative Reconstruction (SAFIRE) is a raw data-
based iterative reconstruction method using a special algorithm.
Compared with the common reconstruction method based on the
same image raw data, the reconstruction with the SAFIRE algorithm
produces images with less noise and enhanced image sharpness.

There are several possibilities for you to plan a recon range:
◾To plan a range quickly but approximately, you can manipulate
range objects in the topo and tomo segments.

job.

In the tomo segment, a recon range is graphically represented as a
square.
The side length of the square indicates the recon FoV (defined by the
FoV parameter). The coordinates of the square's center point

Using HD FoV
Actual analysis shows a HU deviation of nearly +/- 500 HU in the
Extended Field of View of 700 mm. With the Enhanced Extended
Field of View (HD FoV) algorithm, this situation should be improved.
Detecting the patient's contour of the body in combination with an
iterative reconstruction, an HU stability of approximately +/- 20 HU in
the Extended Field of View up to 700 mm can be achieved.

clinical results may vary.

Using extended CT scale
Using an extended CT scale, a wider range of CT values (from -10240
to +30710 Hounsfield units) can be distinguished on images. When
this option is selected, objects with a higher attenuation, such as
metal implants, are shown within the gray scale instead of in white.
◆On the Recon sub-task card, select the Extended CT scale check
box.
Performing 3D recon
To improve workflow efficiency, you can perform 3D image
reconstruction directly on the Recon sub-task card. This is more
convenient than evaluation using the separate 3D task card. You can
reconstruct both MPR and MIP images.
Before you plan a 3D reconstruction, make sure that a spiral scan has
been finished and at least one axial recon job has been finished. The
axial recon images are used as the base images for planning a 3D
reconstruction.
◾Firstly, create a recon job and select 3D as the recon job type on
the Recon sub-task card. An open 3D recon job is indicated by a 3D
recon job icon.
On the 3D recon toolbar, select the desired planning base in the
Planning base list. The axial recon jobs that have been finished
and that are listed before the 3D recon job are available for you to
select.


Images are typically reconstructed in squares, for example, 512
by 512 pixels. If necessary, you can reconstruct non-square
images, by selecting an option from the Matrix size list on the
3D recon toolbar: 512 non-square or 256 non-square. Please
note that the 256 non-square option leads to a reduced image
resolution.
Using FAST 3D
FAST 3D helps you to plan a 3D recon range more efficiently by
automatically completing the following tasks:
◾Detecting the shape of a scanned body part and its z-axis centerline
◾Using the centerline as the 3D recon axis
◾Setting the 3D recon volume (recon starting position, recon ending
position, & FoV) approximately
◾Panning or zooming images in 3D segments
As a result, you see images that can be automatically rotated to fit the
patient's anatomy. In 3D segments, recon range boxes and the FoV
box approximately cover the body region, resulting in no black recon
images. The coronal, axial, and sagittal images are placed in the
segment center and properly sized.
FAST 3D can be turned on in a scan protocol. If a protocol has FAST
3D off, you can still activate it on the Recon sub-task card after the
protocol is loaded into Examination. For any new 3D recon job you
add from the Recon sub-task card, FAST 3D is turned on by default.

Special examination
This section describs information about the following special
examinations :
◾Dual Spiral Dual Energy
◾Veterinary usage
Dual Spiral Dual Energy
The attenuation coefficients of different materials differ under CT
scans of varying energies. This can be exploited to obtain additional
information about the chemical composition of body tissues, for
example, of kidney stones.
Dual Spiral Dual Energy supports a dual-energy exam on a single X-
ray tube CT system. A Dual Spiral Dual Energy exam consists of two
consecutive spiral scans of different voltages.
The same range is scanned twice with different tube voltages: the
first spiral scan uses 80kV; the second spiral scan uses 130kV. The
scan data sets (80kV and 130kV) can be evaluated by using the syngo
Dual Spiral Dual Energy application to visualize information about
anatomical and pathological structures.
CAUTION
Images of Single Source Dual Energy: Inappropriate image
results due to insufficient image registration!
No diagnosis possible.
◆Make sure that the patient does not move between the scans.

A Dual Spiral Dual Energy exam rang is a special kind of auto-range,

130kV.

content:
Contrast examination
CT examinations often involve the intravenous (IV) injection of
contrast medium. Such contrast examinations improve the
characterization of tissue and lesions, as well as increase the opacity
of vessels.
There are 3 methods to carry out a contrast examination:
◾Bolus Tracking
◾TestBolus
◾Fixed delay: the radiologist estimates the scan delay for the
contrast examination.
Contrast timing and volume
For contrast examinations, the exact timing for a scan is essential.
The scan must be performed when the organ or vessel of interest has
the optimal contrast enhancement. Therefore, it is essential to initiate
the scan with an appropriate delay.
In multi-phase examinations, the countdown of the delay starts after
a preceding phase has finished. In the three-phase liver examination,
for example, the scan delay can be set to 600s.
CAUTION
Misunderstanding of reference point for start delay in bolus
examination!
Faulty synchronization between bolus and scanning.
◆Make sure that the chosen delay time fits to the
characteristics of the bolus injection.

content:
CAUTION
Wrong start delay!
X-ray not, or only partially, usable.
◆For acquisition with contrast medium, select the flooding
time of the contrast medium as the delay.
The amount of contrast medium needed depends on the patient’s
weight, circulatory condition, and scan duration. In general, no more
than 3 ml per kg of body weight for adults and 2 ml per kg of body
weight for children should be applied. The scan delay also plays a
role. For a CTA study (the arterial phase), the principle is to keep the
contrast medium flowing for the scan duration. Thus, the contrast
volume can be calculated using the following formula:
Contrast volume = (scan delay + scan duration) × flow rate
Bolus Tracking
Bolus Tracking monitors the flow of contrast medium in a vessel, and
can trigger a diagnostic spiral scan when the vessel enhancement
reaches an optimum level.

◾Use of Bolus Tracking requires a license.
◾The Bolus Tracking feature is also referred to as CARE Bolus.
Workflow of Bolus Tracking
Before you perform Bolus Tracking, make sure that a topogram has
been acquired as usual, and that the parameters for a diagnostic
spiral scan are set up properly.
First, insert the Bolus Tracking steps. You can insert the Bolus
Tracking steps by right-clicking a spiral entry in Chronicle and
choosing Bolus Tracking from the shortcut menu. The Bolus Tracking
steps are added immediately before the spiral entry.

content:
◾Pre-monitoring
◾IV bolus
◾Monitoring
Then, prepare for Bolus Tracking.
In the pre-monitoring step, you acquire an axial image at a reference
slice. The image acquisition uses the sequence mode without any
contrast medium.
The IV Bolus step provides a pause for the injection of contrast
medium. In this step, you place a trigger ROI inside the cross-sectional
view of a vessel on the pre-monitoring image. Contrast enhancement
in the vessel is indicated by an increase in HU at the ROI. You also
activate the auto-trigger option and specify a trigger threshold in HU.
Finally, start Bolus Tracking.
You must start the monitoring step of image acquisitions and start
the injection of contrast medium simultaneously. Scans at the
reference slice and the HU evaluation of the trigger ROI are carried
out repeatedly. When the trigger ROI's HU value reaches the trigger
threshold, the monitoring step stops automatically and its next spiral
scan is triggered.
Inserting Bolus Tracking
1 In Chronicle, right-click a spiral entry.
2 Choose Bolus Tracking from the shortcut menu.

content:
Premonitoring
In the premonitoring step, you acquire an axial image at a reference
slice. The image acquisition uses the sequence mode without any
contrast medium.
The pre-monitoring scan is a single acquisition of a slice image in the
sequence mode for which no contrast medium is used. You need to
position the scan properly to acquire the cross-sectional view of a
vessel, as required for Bolus Tracking.
✓A topogram has been acquired.
1 In Chronicle, select a pre-monitoring entry.
2 To place the pre-monitoring cutline at the proper position, do one
of the following operations on the topogram:
◾To move the cutline, drag the line center.
◾To change the width of the cutline, drag the side handles.

◾When you insert Bolus Tracking steps before a spiral scan, the
pre-monitoring & the monitoring cutlines are positioned, by
default, slightly ahead of the starting position of the spiral
scan. The patient table stays at the cutlines for the Bolus
Tracking procedure. After the procedure, the table does not
have to move to a new position to initiate the spiral scan.
When you drag a cutline towards this default position, the
cutline will snap to the position.

Cardiac examination
The motion of the heart makes it difficult to capture static images. A
cardiac exam monitors a patient's electrocardiograph (ECG) and uses
the ECG signals to control image acquisition. The ECG signals ensure
that images are reconstructed during the same cardiac phase. This
suppresses motion artifacts.
Cardiac examinations are available in two modes:
◾ECG-gated spiral
◾ECG-triggered sequence

The availability of the cardiac function depends on your system
configuration.

Using synthetic ECG
With synthetic trigger/sync, in the case of ECG signal loss during a
scan, the system calculates the sync pulses by averaging over the last
few measured heart beats. A simulated ECG is then used to continue
the scan.
CAUTION
Missing ECG-Sync due to the disconnection of the patient‘s ECG-
electrodes!
X-ray not, or only partially, usable.
◆Check the ECG electrodes before scanning.
◆A contrast enhanced scan should not be aborted but operated
with synthetic ECG-data.
The synthetic trigger/sync option is activated by default for a cardiac
scan. It is recommended that you keep this option always activated
for a scan using contrast medium. If this option is deactivated, a scan
will be aborted in the case of ECG signal loss during the scan.
1 Choose Options > Configuration.
2 Click the HeartView icon.
3 On the General tab, select the ECG Synthetic Trigger/Sync check
box.

If the synthetic trigger/sync option is activated and ECG pulsing is
on, the pulsing will be switched off if the ECG signal is lost during
a scan. Then, the scan dose will be always at the 100% level.

CorCTA spiral
Retrospective ECG gating uses the spiral mode for imaging.
Continuous exposure to radiation is applied for the entire cardiac
cycle over several consecutive heart beats. The ECG is recorded
simultaneously with the spiral data acquisition to allow for
retrospective selection of the cardiac phase for images
reconstruction.
The ECG-gated spiral mode is recommended for patients with
arrhythmia or a higher heart rate.
Setting up ECG pulsing
1 On the Trigger sub-task card, select the ECG Pulsing check box.

CorCTA sequence
Prospective ECG triggering uses the sequence mode for imaging. The
appropriate cardiac phase is used to trigger a scan. To time the
trigger, the mean RR interval of the three preceding heart beats is
used to predict the arrival of the next heart cycle. A reliable prediction
is only possible if the heart rhythm is regular.

Use this dose-saving sequence mode for patients with a lower
and stable heart rate.

Dose report
A dose report is introduced according to the DICOM standard for dose
evaluation purposes.
A dose report can be automatically generated at the end of an
examination and cannot be modified. It is available as a separate
series in Patient Browser.
The dose report uses DICOM terminologies that vary from the phrases
appearing on the user interface of the syngo CT software.
A dose report contains the following information:
◾Patient data
For example, patient name and ID.
◾Administrative data
For example, referring physician and ward number.
◾Dose parameters
For example, CTDlvol and DLP.

◾Examination data

◾Contrast data

◾Scan protocol data
For example, scan type.
◾Dose parameters
For example, CTDIvol.

Archiving patient data
You archive patient data for long-term storage. The data archiving
can be done either by recording patient data to medical grade DVD
discs or by sending the data to the archiving servers on your hospital's
network.
There may be legal regulations pertaining to archiving of digital
image data. The archive operator is responsible for observing these
regulations.
When archiving to network nodes, we strongly recommend the use of
the "Storage Commitment" service. It can be enabled in the Local
Service software, if the remote system supports it.

In case pixel values of the original data exceed the range compatible

lossy compressed during data set conversion.

1 Select the Options > Configurations menu item.
The Somaris/5 – Configuration Panel appears.
2 Double-click the Conversion button.
The DICOM Converter Configuration dialog box appears.
3 Deselect the option Mark images as lossy compressed, if
indispensable, if you do not want images with modified pixel range
to be marked.

As the option Mark images as lossy compressed is activated by
default, images with modified pixel range are labeled with, for
example, CQ!, CF 10 (Compressing Factor 10). If marked as lossy
compressed, images are not accepted for further processing by

HIS/RIS integration
A HIS/RIS system is an integrated information system designed to
manage the administrative, financial, and clinical aspects of a
hospital, and it is used by radiology departments to store,
manipulate, and distribute patient radiological data and imagery.
HIS/RIS system generally consists of patient tracking and scheduling,
result reporting, and image tracking capabilities.

Some manufacturers of Radiology Information Systems (RIS) do
not support the Requested Procedure Description and
Scheduled Procedure Step Description in the Modality
Worklist. In these instances, no information about the kind of
procedure is shown in the worklist. You can contact your RIS
manufacturer for support.
HIS/RIS patient registration
If your CT modality is linked to, licensed, and registered for an HIS/RIS
system, a patient can be registered via the HIS/RIS system. After
registration, the patient information is saved in the Scheduler of
Patient Browser.
MPPS
The exchange of information based on Modality Performed Procedure
Step (MPPS) closes the gap between the modalities and the HIS/RIS.
The information documents which actions have been performed for a
patient. The DICOM worklist, generated in the RIS, was handed over
to the modalities. A MPPS object containing certain information can
be sent back from the modalities to the HIS/RIS.

The purpose of MPPS is to provide features that will help to integrate
the modalities with the supervising information system in the
hospital. Thus a smooth clinical flow is ensured, and billing, dosage,
and other information is generated within the hospital system.
When you register a patient, the system creates an MPPS object. An
MPPS object is generated according to the DICOM Standard for
archiving and evaluation purposes.
If a study is continued with additional scans, a new MPPS is created.
During the examinations and during the post–processing of the
examination results all MPPS relevant information (protocol
information, radiation dose information, film consumption
information, etc.) is automatically filled into the related MPPS object.

◾The MPPS function is available by an optional software license.
If this license is not available, only local MPPS management is
possible, and no feedback is sent to the HIS.
◾Registration by DICOM worklist provides the Scheduled
Procedure Step description. It will be mapped to an existing
scan protocol. If mapping does not exist yet, the study item on
the registration card is empty. To solve this problem, you can
select a scan protocol now to keep the mapping in future.
Select the patient, the examination, or one of the associated series or
images from the Patient Browser; choose Patient > Show MPPS to
open the Modality Performed Procedure Step window.

content:
Quality assurance
To ensure a constantly high image quality, you must perform quality
measurements regularly. Quality tests are usually performed in
several steps:
◾Daily quality measurements
◾Monthly quality measurements (constancy test)
◾Camera test
◾CTDI test (once every six months)
You require the set of phantoms for the quality measurement and
possibly additional accessories for the constancy test.

We recommend having the constancy test performed by Siemens
Healthineers customer service as part of a service contract.
Daily Quality
It is recommended that you perform a quality check of the CT scanner
after long pauses, or whenever ring artifacts occur in images.
The daily quality measurements only require checking of three
parameters on the water phantom:
◾The CT value of water is calculated in Hounsfield units (HU).
◾The Pixel noise of images is calculated as a standard deviation.
◾Tube voltages are measured directly on the x-ray tube.
These measurements are carried out for all available kV values.


All values of the Daily Quality measurements are stored in the
constancy test reports.
Constancy tests
Together with other characteristic values, the daily test values are
checked for constancy monthly. These tests are performed on the
complete set of phantoms. The monthly quality test is performed via
the Quality Constancy dialog box of the Local Service window.
In addition, the CTDI (CT Dose Index) must be measured at least once
every six months. The CTDI must also be measured after any
maintenance work that might have altered the test results.
This section describes how to perfom the following constancy tests:
◾Phantom and phantom position check; Phantom check
◾Position of the lightmarker; Lightmarker
◾Position of the sagittal and coronal lightmarker; Sag/Cor. Lightm
◾Automatic positioning of the tomographic plane using a preview
image; Prev. Image Pos.
◾Real slice thickness; Slice
◾Homogeneity; Homogeneity/Water
◾Pixel noise; Noise
◾Modulation transmission function; MTF
◾Position of the patient table; Table Position
For the monthly constancy test, you require the following phantoms
and accessories:
◾Phantom holder
◾Set of phantoms
◾70 kg (154 lb) weight
◾Ruler, 300 mm or longer

MTF test
The spatial resolution is characterized through the modulation
transmission function (MTF). It describes the contrast amplitude of
bar patterns with different local frequencies shown in the image
relative to an ideal transmission.
The 2 % value of the MTF is the local frequency at which the contrast
of periodical bar patterns of this local frequency is reduced to 2 %. In
practice, the MTF values are determined using a single thin wire.
After the previous test has been completed, the MTF test is started
automatically.
◆Press the Start key on the control box, if prompted.
Scanning is started.
The MTF is represented graphically as a function of the local
frequency (LP/cm). In addition, three characteristic values, 50 %
MTF, 10 % MTF and 2 % MTF are displayed.
The scan is displayed in the image area. The result image is
calculated and stored in the local database.

The Low Contrast test is performed in the Quality Constancy dialog



The low contrast phantom section consists of a 165 mm diameter, 25

low contrast differences between the pins and the surrounding area.

Monitor test requirement
Constancy test requirements for image display devices (monitors)
may vary according to different national regulations. The constancy
test described herein complies with the German X-ray regulations
(Deutsche Roentgenverordnung) and is based on requirements given
in DIN V 6868-57.
CAUTION
Missing constancy test of the monitor!
Wrong basis for diagnosis.
◆Perform the monitor test regularly at the recommended
intervals.
The acceptance test performed during initial start-up commissioning
ensures optimum image quality of the device. The results of these
measurements are documented in an acceptance test report and
serve as reference values for the follow-up constancy test.
If any alterations are made to the device that affect the image quality,
for example, repairs, replacement of parts, or readjustments, the
acceptance test according to the Germany X-ray regulations must be
repeated.
Monitor test equipment
The constancy test is performed using the following test equipment:
◾Luminance meter for LCD monitors
Specification: Class B (DIN 5032-7) with valid calibration, range
0.05 cd/m2 – 1000cd/m2 (recommended device: Spotmeter SMfit
Act for LCD monitors)
◾Test image source (imaging device)
◾Test images

ePatch Sensor CE Instructions for Use   
 5 OF 43 
02-01556 Rev N 
 
1 Description, indications for use, contraindications, warnings, 
and precautions 
Please read these instructions carefully before using the ePatch Sensor (later termed Sensor) or any of 
the accessories. Contact the healthcare professional or product customer service in your country with 
any questions. 
 
1.1 Description 
The ePatch Sensor (later termed Sensor) is intended for continuous recording of heart action potentials 
(ECG). While in use, the Sensor is connected to a compatible ECG Electrode accessory (later termed 
ECG Electrode), such as an ECG Electrode Patch (later termed Patch) and placed on the patient. 
The Sensor interfaces with a compatible Charge Adapter. The Sensor is rechargeable and reusable. 
The Sensor contains internal non-volatile storage that stores the ECG data until the file with the ECG 
data is deleted. The Sensor contains embedded software for recording ECG, storing ECG, and 
charging. When the Sensor is connected to a PC through the Charge Adapter, the recorded ECG files 
are accessible as a USB mass storage device. 
There are two (2) models of the ePatch Sensor: 
• 
REF ePatch 2.0 
• 
REF 02-02046 
 
1.2 Indications for use 
ePatch Sensor is indicated for use on patients who may be asymptomatic or who may suffer from 
transient symptoms such as palpitations, shortness of breath, dizziness, light headedness, pre-syncope, 
syncope, fatigue, chest pain and/or anxiety. 
The Sensor is intended for use by adolescents 18-21 and adults. 
 
1.3 Intended Users/Intended Use Environment 
 
Intended Users: Healthcare professionals (e.g., Physicians, nurses) and lay-users (patients and their 
respective care givers). 
 
Intended Use Environment: The Sensor is intended for use in hospital/health care facilities and in a 
home setting. 
 
1.4 Intended Population 
The ePatch Sensor is intended for use by adolescents 18-21 and adults.

cause a choking hazard or cause suffocation if placed over face or mouth. There is a danger
of strangulation if the provided USB Cable and/or lead wires are misused.

specific Warnings.

chunk_id: Copy of Epatch Sensor Ce Instructions For U_p7_t7
content:
The ePatch System is indicated for patients 18 years of age and older. Its safety and effectiveness
have not been evaluated in patients who are outside of the indicated patient population and use may
be associated with risks including the potential for inaccurate data capture, skin sensitivity, or other
adverse consequences.
Do not use a broken Sensor. This can cause electric discharge or decrease the quality of the acquired
ECG signals.
Do not touch the terminals at the backside of the Sensor or let them touch other conductive parts or
earth. This may damage the Sensor.
If the Sensor is not firmly connected to the ECG Electrode Patch, it is not splash proof (Protection level
IP24). To avoid malfunction, make sure both parts are firmly connected with no gaps and do not expose
to direct jet of water or liquid.
Do not expose the internal parts of the Sensor, the Charge Adapter, or the AC Adapter to any liquids.
Do not submerge the Sensor, the Charge Adapter, or the AC Adapter in any liquid. This may cause
electric short circuiting or electrical discharge.
Minimize the number of devices connected to the patient. Otherwise, there is a risk of accumulation of
leakage current.
Store and use the Sensor within temperature, pressure, and humidity ranges specified in Section
10.1.4.
Avoid exposing any part of the Sensor to heat sources, heat radiators and fireplaces, direct exposure
to sunlight, nebulizers, or electrical steam kettles. Temperature changes cause condensation and
moisture that can lead to malfunction of the Sensor.
Before using the Sensor, allow it to acclimate to ambient temperature. For reference, if the temperature
difference between the Sensor and the environment is above 10ºC, A 20-minutes wait time in an
intermediate temperature is recommended.
Mobile phones, transmitters, and similar equipment generating radio frequency (RF) emissions should
not be placed next to the Sensor during use. This can affect the Sensor. Follow the recommendations
regarding the separation distance specified in the manufacturer’s declaration for EMC in this
Instructions For Use document, see Annex 1.
Do not lie directly on the Sensor.
Do not connect the Sensor to external electrical equipment.
Please refer to the Instructions for Use associated with the compatible accessory for their specific
Precautions.

ePatch Sensor CE Instructions for Use   
 16 OF 43 
02-01556 Rev N 
 
Step 4: Prepare the skin (when using the ECG Electrode Patch) 
Do not place the Patch on broken, damaged, or irritated skin. Apply the Patch ONLY on 
clean intact skin and NEVER on open wounds, lesions, infected or inflamed areas. 
Expose the chest and prepare the skin according to the steps below. Example illustrations for slanted 
position serve as guidance for proper technique. 
 
1. Determine the chest area needing to be prepared by referring to the 
diagram. Locate the collarbone on the left side of the body and 
measure three (3) finger widths down (when using a slanted 
position) or three (3) finger widths below the upper rim of the 
sternum (vertical) (when using a sternum (vertical) position). 
 
2. If hair is on the chest, wash and shave the area where the Patch 
will be placed. Start at the center of the chest and shave the entire 
area marked in the red circle of the diagram. 
 
 
 
 
3. Clean the area with soap and water. 
 
4. Dry skin thoroughly using a towel. 
 
5. Gently rub the skin using the scrub pad (if provided) in a circular 
motion for 1 minute. This step may help in providing a better ECG 
signal. 
 
 
6. It is important to wait for a minimum of 2-3 minutes until the skin is 
completely dry before applying the Patch. While waiting, continue to 
the next steps. 
NOTE: Do not apply oils or lotions in the cleaned area before attaching the Patch to the skin. The 
quality of the signals might be decreased if the skin is not properly prepared.

Step 5: Connect the Sensor and the ECG Electrode Patch (when using the ECG 
Electrode Patch) 
NOTE: Do not connect the Sensor and the Patch until after skin preparation. The Sensor powers on 
and starts the recording within five (5) minutes after it has been connected to the Patch. Premature 
connection may therefore shorten the length of the recording time. 
Follow the steps below for either model of ECG Electrode Patch. Example illustrations serve as 
guidance for proper technique. 
 
1. Peel open the packaging and remove the Patch.   
 
2. Always check the use by date on the packaging of the Patch before 
use.  
 
3. Do not open the Patch packaging until the Patch is to be used. 
Otherwise, the adhesive material might dry. 
 
4. Place the Sensor onto the blue plastic cradle of the Patch. 
 
5. Press down firmly as shown to snap the Sensor in place. Ensure no 
gaps are visible between parts. You will hear several clicks. 
 
 
 
6. Once connected, a constant green light will appear followed by a 
flashing green light (for about 30 seconds) indicating the Sensor is 
working. The recording will automatically start when the flashing 
green light stops. 
Correct- No Gap 
7. To avoid malfunction, visually inspect and make sure both parts are 
firmly connected with no gaps. 
 
CAUTION: If the Sensor is not firmly connected to the Patch, it is not 
splash proof. This may cause ingress of liquids to the internal parts of 
the Sensor which may result in electrical short circuiting and 
malfunction of the Sensor.  
Incorrect- Gap 
8. If gaps are visible between the Sensor and the Patch, press the two 
items firmly together to close the gaps.

Prepare the skin 
Expose the chest and prepare the skin according to the steps below 
 
1. Determine the chest area needing to be prepared by referring to

electrodes will be placed. 
 
3. Clean the area with soap and water 
 
4. Dry skin thoroughly using a towel 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5. It is important to wait for a minimum of 2-3 minutes until the skin 
is completely dry before proceeding to the next step.  
NOTE: Do not apply oils or lotions in the cleaned areas before attaching the electrodes to the skin. The 
quality of the ECG signals may be decreased if the skin is not properly prepared. 
 
Step 11: Connect the Sensor and the Flex Adapter (when using the Flex Adapter)    
 
1. Slide the Sensor into the Flex Adapter. A green light on the Sensor 
will flash briefly when the Sensor is completely inserted. 
 
2. Once connected, a constant green light will appear followed by a 
flashing green light (for about 30 seconds) indicating the Sensor is

CAUTION: 
Do not swim while wearing the ePatch Sensor and ECG Electrode 
Patch/LWA /Flex Adapter. Do not submerge ePatch Sensor in any form of liquid. Fully 
immersing may render the Sensor inoperable, may cause recorded ECG data to be 
unreadable, or may affect proper functionality. 
5 What to remember during recording and use 
 
 
Showering 
If the ePatch Sensor is not firmly connected to the Patch, it is not splash proof. When 
the Sensor is properly inserted into the Patch, water splashing against the enclosure 
from any direction will have no harmful effect. While showering, it is recommended 
to face away from the shower head and deflect any direct showering water from 
impinging on the Sensor by shielding it away from the direct spray of the shower with 
a hand or a cloth. 
 
Do not swim or submerge the Sensor in water or liquids. The Sensor is water resistant when combined 
with the Patch, but it is not waterproof.     
 
For the LWA Set-up: The Sensor is NOT water resistant when worn with the LWA; 
therefore, do not shower, bathe or swim while wearing the Sensor in the LWA Set-up.  
 
Before showering/bathing/swimming, unsnap the leads from the surface electrodes, 
remove the surface electrodes from skin, remove LWA with Sensor and set aside.  
 
 
For the Flex Adapter Set-up: The Sensor is NOT water resistant when worn with the 
Flex Adapter; therefore, do not bathe or swim while wearing the Sensor in the Flex 
Adapter Set-up.  
 
Before showering, unsnap the surface electrodes from the Flex Adapter, remove the 
surface electrodes from skin, and set aside the Sensor and Flex Adapter.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
After a shower 
Patch Set-up: After taking a shower, always inspect the Sensor to Patch connection, and adhesion of 
the Patch to the skin. If needed, replace Patch. Continued use of a damaged ECG Electrode Patch 
may affect quality of ECG measurements. Please follow the instructions in Chapter 4. 
LWA Set-up: Reapply new surface electrodes and re-attach the lead wire. Please follow the instructions 
in Chapter 4. 
Flex Adapter Set-up: Reapply new surface electrodes and re-attach the Flex Adapter. Please follow the 
instructions in Chapter 4.

Activities 
Activities that result in excessive sweating might loosen the Patch, or cause gel to leak out. If this occurs, 
remove and replace the Patch by following instructions in Chapter 7 for removal, and in Chapter 4 for 
applying a new Patch. 
 
Skin irritation 
Minor discomfort, skin irritation, reddening, itching, or rash can occur by use of the ePatch Sensor system. 
Any sign of severe skin irritation or allergy should be reported to the healthcare professional and closely 
monitored to avoid development of more serious reactions. 
 
6 Perform an Event Marker 
The healthcare professional may ask you to perform a digital event marker in the recorded ECG data 
file (if enabled). The digital event marker is an optional functionality that provides a means to mark an 
event with a timestamp if a health-related symptom is felt. The use of this functionality will not result in 
loss of data and will have no impact on the data monitoring function of the ePatch Sensor.  
 
How to perform an Event Marker 
Double tap the middle of the Sensor rapidly (within one (1) second) and the status indicator on the 
Sensor will show a constant green light for one (1) second. 
 
When to perform an Event Marker 
Examples of when an Event Marker can be performed: 
• 
When feeling shortness of breath 
• 
When feeling chest pain 
• 
When feeling dizziness 
• 
When feeling palpitations 
 
Symptom Event Diary 
You may be asked to fill in a symptom event diary to record your activities and 
symptoms. Be sure to include the day and time that your monitoring period had 
started on the front page. 
Whenever you experience a symptom, be sure to write the day and time of its 
occurrence in the symptom event diary.

- 
If persists, call Customer Service. 
 
If you are a healthcare professional, follow these steps: 
- 
Ensure that the Sensor is correctly connected to a 
compatible ECG Electrode Patch or LWA (See Chapter 4). 
- 
Ensure that the Sensor is fully charged (see Chapter 4). 
 
NOTE: Remember that the flashing green light stops 
automatically once the recording starts (up to five (5) minutes after 
the Sensor and the ECG Electrode Patch or LWA were 
connected). 
The Sensor does not show a 
green light to acknowledge the 
marking of an event 
- 
The green light turns on briefly for one (1) second when 
receiving an event marking. When marking an event, look 
closely at the Sensor (preferably in front of a mirror) to 
ensure that the green light is seen. 
- 
Try double-tapping again with a higher tapping frequency. 
You should tap it twice within one (1) second. 
- 
Try double-tapping again with increased firmness. 
- 
If using a Patch, ensure that the Sensor is firmly connected 
to the Patch with no gaps. 
- 
If using an LWA, ensure that the Sensor is firmly in place. 
- 
If using a Flex Adapter, ensure that the Sensor is completely 
inserted. 
- 
If it is still not possible to mark an event, the Sensor may 
have stopped recording due to the predefined recording 
time having elapsed, or the event marker function may have 
been disabled in the Sensor. 
Irritated or reddened skin 
- 
You may be experiencing an allergic reaction to the 
adhesive of the Patch. If you experience irritation worse 
than minor itching, contact your healthcare professional. 
Patch comes loose from skin 
- 
Stick the Patch back on your skin by pressing down the 
adhesive edges. 
- 
If that does not work, contact your healthcare professional, 
you may need to replace the Patch. 
Gel leaking out of Patch 
- 
Remove the Patch by following instructions in Chapter 7 for 
removal. 
- 
Place new Patch by following instructions in Chapter 4 for 
applying a new Patch.

9 
Cleaning, disinfection, maintenance, and disposal 
NOTE: The information in this section is to be used by professionals processing Sensors for use on the 
next patient. 
Do not reuse single use accessories.  
For cleaning instructions for a specific reusable accessory (see accessories in Chapter 3), refer to the 
accessory Instructions For Use document. 
 
9.1 
Cleaning & Disinfection Before/After Patient Use 
NOTE: Follow the instructions described in this section to clean and disinfect the 
Sensor in the following situations, in order to prevent cross contamination: 
• 
After use of the Sensor on a patient.   
• 
Prior to placing the Sensor in a Charge Adapter (make sure Sensor is 
visibly dry before placement in a Charge Adapter).  
• 
Prior to use of the Sensor on the next patient.  
 
NOTE: Wear protective gloves when handling Sensors returned from patients, during cleaning and 
disinfection. 
 
Step 1: Prepare Sensor 
Separate the Sensor from any ECG Electrode accessory (Patch blue cradle, Lead Wire Adapter or Flex 
Adapter), or remove the Sensor from the Charge Adapter.  
 
Step 2: Remove Debris and Clean 
1. Examine the Sensor enclosure and look for any visible residue, debris, stains, discoloration 
or marks on the Sensor. Pay close attention to the crevices at the edges of electrical contact, 
inside corners of the back case ribs, and any areas of the Sensor where debris may 
accumulate such as the blue seal area (refer to images a, b and c below in Step 3). 
2. If you notice any visible residue, debris, stains, discoloration or marks on the Sensor, remove 
those with an acetone-free cleaning agent such as Medline Adhesive Remover Pads (not 
supplied with the Sensor). If still present, use a combination of an acetone-free cleaning 
agent, a latex free erase, and/or a plastic razor blade (not supplied with the Sensor).  
3. Rub the entire Sensor enclosure with a prepared 70% Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA) solution (not 
supplied with the Sensor). Pay close attention to the Sensor’s blue seal (refer to image c 
below) and wipe it entirely. You may use any of these application forms: 
a. A wipe saturated in 70% IPA but not dripping 
b. A dampened soft cloth saturated in 70% IPA but not dripping  
c. Directly spray the Sensor with 70% IPA mist and use a clean, soft cloth to wipe 
4. Visually inspect the Sensor for residue, debris, stains, discoloration or marks. If any are 
visible, repeat the steps in this section as necessary.

ePatch Sensor CE Instructions for Use   
 34 OF 43 
02-01556 Rev N 
 
9.2 
Maintenance 
There are no serviceable parts on the Sensor or on its compatible accessories and components.  
 
9.2.1 Preventative Maintenance 
Check periodically that the Sensor and its compatible accessories and components are not broken, have 
no external damage, and that the performance is acceptable (i.e., length of recording has not diminished 
from a fully charged battery). 
If issues are detected that cannot be solved, please contact Braemar Manufacturing, LLC. or the product 
Customer Service in your country. 
During transportation, storage, and between uses, it is recommended to store the Sensor, the Charge 
Adapter, and the AC Adapter in the provided packaging. Only use the Sensor with compatible accessories 
supplied by the manufacturer.  
 
9.2.2 Corrective Maintenance 
If the Sensor presents an issue that prevents normal operation and that cannot be solved after consulting 
the Troubleshooting section (Chapter 8), please contact Customer Support or your distributor, and specify 
the type of problem. 
 
9.2.3 Calibration 
The Sensor and its compatible accessories and component do not require calibration. 
 
9.2.4 Disposal  
The Sensor is reusable and should be returned by the patient at the conclusion of the predefined 
recording time to the prescribing physician, or by mailing back the Sensor in a return envelope if provided 
by the physician. 
For disposal instructions for a specific accessory, refer to the accessory IFU (see Chapter 3 for list of 
accessories). 
 
9.2.5 Disposal of Electrical and Electronic Devices  
Never dispose of the Sensor, the Charge Adapter or the AC Adapter in the household trash. It must 
be disposed of properly and may need to be recycled in accordance with the statutory requirements in 
your area. Information on proper disposal is available from your distributor.

Example configuration for a 3-channel recording 
 
The Patch has three (3) active electrodes and channels can be created between electrodes 1, 2 or 3 in any 
combination.  
 
 
Lead Wire Adapter Configuration 
 
   
 
The Lead Wire Adapter utilizes three (3) electrodes. Channel 1 is formed by the white electrode (1 Right Arm) 
and black electrode (2 Left Arm), Channel 2 is formed by the white electrode (1 Right Arm) and the red electrode 
(3 Lower Left) and Channel 3 is formed by the black electrode (2 Left Arm) and the red electrode (3 Lower Left).  
 
Electrode 1 is the common electrode to channel 1 and channel 2. 
 
 
Flex Adapter Configuration 
 
 
 
 
 
The Flex Adapter utilizes two electrodes. Channels 1 and 2 are formed by Electrodes 1 and 2. Channel 1 and 
channel 2 are connected in parallel. 
 
Electrode 1 is the common electrode to channel 1 and channel 2.

ePatch Sensor CE Instructions for Use   
 5 OF 43 
02-01556 Rev N 
 
1 Description, indications for use, contraindications, warnings, 
and precautions 
Please read these instructions carefully before using the ePatch Sensor (later termed Sensor) or any of 
the accessories. Contact the healthcare professional or product customer service in your country with 
any questions. 
 
1.1 Description 
The ePatch Sensor (later termed Sensor) is intended for continuous recording of heart action potentials 
(ECG). While in use, the Sensor is connected to a compatible ECG Electrode accessory (later termed 
ECG Electrode), such as an ECG Electrode Patch (later termed Patch) and placed on the patient. 
The Sensor interfaces with a compatible Charge Adapter. The Sensor is rechargeable and reusable. 
The Sensor contains internal non-volatile storage that stores the ECG data until the file with the ECG 
data is deleted. The Sensor contains embedded software for recording ECG, storing ECG, and 
charging. When the Sensor is connected to a PC through the Charge Adapter, the recorded ECG files 
are accessible as a USB mass storage device. 
There are two (2) models of the ePatch Sensor: 
• 
REF ePatch 2.0 
• 
REF 02-02046 
 
1.2 Indications for use 
ePatch Sensor is indicated for use on patients who may be asymptomatic or who may suffer from 
transient symptoms such as palpitations, shortness of breath, dizziness, light headedness, pre-syncope, 
syncope, fatigue, chest pain and/or anxiety. 
The Sensor is intended for use by adolescents 18-21 and adults. 
 
1.3 Intended Users/Intended Use Environment 
 
Intended Users: Healthcare professionals (e.g., Physicians, nurses) and lay-users (patients and their 
respective care givers). 
 
Intended Use Environment: The Sensor is intended for use in hospital/health care facilities and in a 
home setting. 
 
1.4 Intended Population 
The ePatch Sensor is intended for use by adolescents 18-21 and adults.

The Sensor has not been evaluated to support its use on infants, or on pregnant and/or
breastfeeding women.
The Sensor is not intended for use on patients with an implanted pacemaker or an Implantable
Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD).
Do not use the Sensor in an X-ray, computed tomography (CT), or magnetic resonance
imaging (MRI) environment. This may affect the scanning results, may lead to malfunction of
the Sensor, and it may injure the patient.
Remove Sensor prior to defibrillation.
Do not tamper with, disassemble or modify Sensor or accessories, as this may affect
functionality or performance. A slight electrical sensation may be experienced.
Use the Sensor with compatible accessories supplied by the manufacturer. Otherwise,
electrical shock or damage to the Sensor may occur. In addition, the ECG signal quality could
be affected.
Use of other equipment or accessories not specified in this Instructions For Use document
might lead to skin irritations, allergy, electrical shock, and malfunction of the Sensor. Use of
other chargers may damage the device and/or the accessories.
Keep products out of reach of unsupervised infants, children and pets, as this could potentially
cause a choking hazard or cause suffocation if placed over face or mouth. There is a danger
of strangulation if the provided USB Cable and/or lead wires are misused.
Please refer to the Instructions for Use associated with the compatible accessory for their
specific Warnings.

chunk_id: Copy of Epatch Sensor Ce Instructions For U_1_p7_t7
content:
The ePatch System is indicated for patients 18 years of age and older. Its safety and effectiveness
have not been evaluated in patients who are outside of the indicated patient population and use may
be associated with risks including the potential for inaccurate data capture, skin sensitivity, or other
adverse consequences.
Do not use a broken Sensor. This can cause electric discharge or decrease the quality of the acquired
ECG signals.
Do not touch the terminals at the backside of the Sensor or let them touch other conductive parts or
earth. This may damage the Sensor.
If the Sensor is not firmly connected to the ECG Electrode Patch, it is not splash proof (Protection level
IP24). To avoid malfunction, make sure both parts are firmly connected with no gaps and do not expose
to direct jet of water or liquid.
Do not expose the internal parts of the Sensor, the Charge Adapter, or the AC Adapter to any liquids.
Do not submerge the Sensor, the Charge Adapter, or the AC Adapter in any liquid. This may cause
electric short circuiting or electrical discharge.
Minimize the number of devices connected to the patient. Otherwise, there is a risk of accumulation of
leakage current.
Store and use the Sensor within temperature, pressure, and humidity ranges specified in Section
10.1.4.
Avoid exposing any part of the Sensor to heat sources, heat radiators and fireplaces, direct exposure
to sunlight, nebulizers, or electrical steam kettles. Temperature changes cause condensation and
moisture that can lead to malfunction of the Sensor.
Before using the Sensor, allow it to acclimate to ambient temperature. For reference, if the temperature
difference between the Sensor and the environment is above 10ºC, A 20-minutes wait time in an
intermediate temperature is recommended.
Mobile phones, transmitters, and similar equipment generating radio frequency (RF) emissions should
not be placed next to the Sensor during use. This can affect the Sensor. Follow the recommendations
regarding the separation distance specified in the manufacturer’s declaration for EMC in this
Instructions For Use document, see Annex 1.
Do not lie directly on the Sensor.
Do not connect the Sensor to external electrical equipment.
Please refer to the Instructions for Use associated with the compatible accessory for their specific
Precautions.

Step 4: Prepare the skin (when using the ECG Electrode Patch) 
Do not place the Patch on broken, damaged, or irritated skin. Apply the Patch ONLY on 
clean intact skin and NEVER on open wounds, lesions, infected or inflamed areas. 
Expose the chest and prepare the skin according to the steps below. Example illustrations for slanted 
position serve as guidance for proper technique. 
 
1. Determine the chest area needing to be prepared by referring to the 
diagram. Locate the collarbone on the left side of the body and 
measure three (3) finger widths down (when using a slanted 
position) or three (3) finger widths below the upper rim of the 
sternum (vertical) (when using a sternum (vertical) position). 
 
2. If hair is on the chest, wash and shave the area where the Patch 
will be placed. Start at the center of the chest and shave the entire 
area marked in the red circle of the diagram. 
 
 
 
 
3. Clean the area with soap and water. 
 
4. Dry skin thoroughly using a towel. 
 
5. Gently rub the skin using the scrub pad (if provided) in a circular 
motion for 1 minute. This step may help in providing a better ECG 
signal. 
 
 
6. It is important to wait for a minimum of 2-3 minutes until the skin is 
completely dry before applying the Patch. While waiting, continue to 
the next steps. 
NOTE: Do not apply oils or lotions in the cleaned area before attaching the Patch to the skin. The 
quality of the signals might be decreased if the skin is not properly prepared.

Step 5: Connect the Sensor and the ECG Electrode Patch (when using the ECG 
Electrode Patch) 
NOTE: Do not connect the Sensor and the Patch until after skin preparation. The Sensor powers on 
and starts the recording within five (5) minutes after it has been connected to the Patch. Premature 
connection may therefore shorten the length of the recording time. 
Follow the steps below for either model of ECG Electrode Patch. Example illustrations serve as 
guidance for proper technique. 
 
1. Peel open the packaging and remove the Patch.   
 
2. Always check the use by date on the packaging of the Patch before 
use.  
 
3. Do not open the Patch packaging until the Patch is to be used. 
Otherwise, the adhesive material might dry. 
 
4. Place the Sensor onto the blue plastic cradle of the Patch. 
 
5. Press down firmly as shown to snap the Sensor in place. Ensure no 
gaps are visible between parts. You will hear several clicks. 
 
 
 
6. Once connected, a constant green light will appear followed by a 
flashing green light (for about 30 seconds) indicating the Sensor is 
working. The recording will automatically start when the flashing 
green light stops. 
Correct- No Gap 
7. To avoid malfunction, visually inspect and make sure both parts are 
firmly connected with no gaps. 
 
CAUTION: If the Sensor is not firmly connected to the Patch, it is not 
splash proof. This may cause ingress of liquids to the internal parts of 
the Sensor which may result in electrical short circuiting and 
malfunction of the Sensor.  
Incorrect- Gap 
8. If gaps are visible between the Sensor and the Patch, press the two 
items firmly together to close the gaps.

1. Slide the Sensor into the Flex Adapter. A green light on the Sensor 
will flash briefly when the Sensor is completely inserted. 
 
2. Once connected, a constant green light will appear followed by a 
flashing green light (for about 30 seconds) indicating the Sensor is 
working.

CAUTION: 
Do not swim while wearing the ePatch Sensor and ECG Electrode 
Patch/LWA /Flex Adapter. Do not submerge ePatch Sensor in any form of liquid. Fully 
immersing may render the Sensor inoperable, may cause recorded ECG data to be 
unreadable, or may affect proper functionality. 
5 What to remember during recording and use 
 
 
Showering 
If the ePatch Sensor is not firmly connected to the Patch, it is not splash proof. When 
the Sensor is properly inserted into the Patch, water splashing against the enclosure 
from any direction will have no harmful effect. While showering, it is recommended 
to face away from the shower head and deflect any direct showering water from 
impinging on the Sensor by shielding it away from the direct spray of the shower with 
a hand or a cloth. 
 
Do not swim or submerge the Sensor in water or liquids. The Sensor is water resistant when combined 
with the Patch, but it is not waterproof.     
 
For the LWA Set-up: The Sensor is NOT water resistant when worn with the LWA; 
therefore, do not shower, bathe or swim while wearing the Sensor in the LWA Set-up.  
 
Before showering/bathing/swimming, unsnap the leads from the surface electrodes, 
remove the surface electrodes from skin, remove LWA with Sensor and set aside.  
 
 
For the Flex Adapter Set-up: The Sensor is NOT water resistant when worn with the 
Flex Adapter; therefore, do not bathe or swim while wearing the Sensor in the Flex 
Adapter Set-up.  
 
Before showering, unsnap the surface electrodes from the Flex Adapter, remove the 
surface electrodes from skin, and set aside the Sensor and Flex Adapter.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
After a shower 
Patch Set-up: After taking a shower, always inspect the Sensor to Patch connection, and adhesion of 
the Patch to the skin. If needed, replace Patch. Continued use of a damaged ECG Electrode Patch 
may affect quality of ECG measurements. Please follow the instructions in Chapter 4. 
LWA Set-up: Reapply new surface electrodes and re-attach the lead wire. Please follow the instructions 
in Chapter 4. 
Flex Adapter Set-up: Reapply new surface electrodes and re-attach the Flex Adapter. Please follow the 
instructions in Chapter 4.

Activities 
Activities that result in excessive sweating might loosen the Patch, or cause gel to leak out. If this occurs, 
remove and replace the Patch by following instructions in Chapter 7 for removal, and in Chapter 4 for 
applying a new Patch. 
 
Skin irritation 
Minor discomfort, skin irritation, reddening, itching, or rash can occur by use of the ePatch Sensor system. 
Any sign of severe skin irritation or allergy should be reported to the healthcare professional and closely 
monitored to avoid development of more serious reactions. 
 
6 Perform an Event Marker 
The healthcare professional may ask you to perform a digital event marker in the recorded ECG data 
file (if enabled). The digital event marker is an optional functionality that provides a means to mark an 
event with a timestamp if a health-related symptom is felt. The use of this functionality will not result in 
loss of data and will have no impact on the data monitoring function of the ePatch Sensor.  
 
How to perform an Event Marker 
Double tap the middle of the Sensor rapidly (within one (1) second) and the status indicator on the 
Sensor will show a constant green light for one (1) second. 
 
When to perform an Event Marker 
Examples of when an Event Marker can be performed: 
• 
When feeling shortness of breath 
• 
When feeling chest pain 
• 
When feeling dizziness 
• 
When feeling palpitations 
 
Symptom Event Diary 
You may be asked to fill in a symptom event diary to record your activities and 
symptoms. Be sure to include the day and time that your monitoring period had 
started on the front page. 
Whenever you experience a symptom, be sure to write the day and time of its 
occurrence in the symptom event diary.

next patient. 
Do not reuse single use accessories.  
For cleaning instructions for a specific reusable accessory (see accessories in Chapter 3), refer to the 
accessory Instructions For Use document. 
 
9.1 
Cleaning & Disinfection Before/After Patient Use 
NOTE: Follow the instructions described in this section to clean and disinfect the 
Sensor in the following situations, in order to prevent cross contamination: 
• 
After use of the Sensor on a patient.   
• 
Prior to placing the Sensor in a Charge Adapter (make sure Sensor is 
visibly dry before placement in a Charge Adapter).  
• 
Prior to use of the Sensor on the next patient.  
 
NOTE: Wear protective gloves when handling Sensors returned from patients, during cleaning and 
disinfection. 
 
Step 1: Prepare Sensor 
Separate the Sensor from any ECG Electrode accessory (Patch blue cradle, Lead Wire Adapter or Flex 
Adapter), or remove the Sensor from the Charge Adapter.  
 
Step 2: Remove Debris and Clean 
1. Examine the Sensor enclosure and look for any visible residue, debris, stains, discoloration 
or marks on the Sensor. Pay close attention to the crevices at the edges of electrical contact, 
inside corners of the back case ribs, and any areas of the Sensor where debris may 
accumulate such as the blue seal area (refer to images a, b and c below in Step 3). 
2. If you notice any visible residue, debris, stains, discoloration or marks on the Sensor, remove 
those with an acetone-free cleaning agent such as Medline Adhesive Remover Pads (not 
supplied with the Sensor). If still present, use a combination of an acetone-free cleaning 
agent, a latex free erase, and/or a plastic razor blade (not supplied with the Sensor).  
3. Rub the entire Sensor enclosure with a prepared 70% Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA) solution (not 
supplied with the Sensor). Pay close attention to the Sensor’s blue seal (refer to image c 
below) and wipe it entirely. You may use any of these application forms: 
a. A wipe saturated in 70% IPA but not dripping 
b. A dampened soft cloth saturated in 70% IPA but not dripping  
c. Directly spray the Sensor with 70% IPA mist and use a clean, soft cloth to wipe 
4. Visually inspect the Sensor for residue, debris, stains, discoloration or marks. If any are 
visible, repeat the steps in this section as necessary.

ePatch Sensor CE Instructions for Use

02-01556 Rev N 
 
9.2 
Maintenance 
There are no serviceable parts on the Sensor or on its compatible accessories and components.  
 
9.2.1 Preventative Maintenance 
Check periodically that the Sensor and its compatible accessories and components are not broken, have 
no external damage, and that the performance is acceptable (i.e., length of recording has not diminished 
from a fully charged battery). 
If issues are detected that cannot be solved, please contact Braemar Manufacturing, LLC. or the product 
Customer Service in your country. 
During transportation, storage, and between uses, it is recommended to store the Sensor, the Charge 
Adapter, and the AC Adapter in the provided packaging. Only use the Sensor with compatible accessories 
supplied by the manufacturer.  
 
9.2.2 Corrective Maintenance 
If the Sensor presents an issue that prevents normal operation and that cannot be solved after consulting 
the Troubleshooting section (Chapter 8), please contact Customer Support or your distributor, and specify 
the type of problem. 
 
9.2.3 Calibration 
The Sensor and its compatible accessories and component do not require calibration. 
 
9.2.4 Disposal  
The Sensor is reusable and should be returned by the patient at the conclusion of the predefined 
recording time to the prescribing physician, or by mailing back the Sensor in a return envelope if provided 
by the physician. 
For disposal instructions for a specific accessory, refer to the accessory IFU (see Chapter 3 for list of 
accessories). 
 
9.2.5 Disposal of Electrical and Electronic Devices  
Never dispose of the Sensor, the Charge Adapter or the AC Adapter in the household trash. It must 
be disposed of properly and may need to be recycled in accordance with the statutory requirements in 
your area. Information on proper disposal is available from your distributor.

content:
G30/40 Patient Monitors Service Guide
7
Safety Requirements
Note — The safety indications in this chapter apply to general monitor use. Safety indications in other 
chapters apply to specific monitor measurements. 
Follow the instructions of this service guide when using the monitor. However, conventional medical practices 
always supersede this document. Significance of safety requirements set forth here in this manual is not in 
order of reading sequence.
Warning
Never rely exclusively on the alarm system for patient monitoring. Low alarm limits or turning the alarm 
off during patient monitoring may result in patient danger. The most reliable method of patient 
monitoring combines close, personal surveillance along with the correct operation of the monitor. You 
must periodically check that monitor alarms are working properly.
Only use the monitor on one patient at a time.
Never use the monitor to monitor apnea.
Anyone who connects additional equipment to the signal input port or signal output port configures a 
medical system and is therefore responsible to ensure that the system complies with the requirements of 
standard IEC 60601-1. Never permanently install equipment connected to the signal input or output 
ports. If in doubt, contact Philips Goldway.
The monitor is not for home use. 
The monitor is not for diagnostic or therapeutic use.
To avoid confusing patient records, clear all historical data of the last patient before monitoring a new 
patient. 
To avoid personal injury, only use accessories and parts produced or recommended by Philips Goldway.
Ensure that the monitor is in good working condition and is placed in the proper position before 
monitoring a new patient.
For pacemaker patients, rate meters may continue to count the pacemaker rate during occurrences of 
cardiac arrest or arrhythmia. Do not rely entirely on rate meter alarms. Keep pacemaker patients under 
close curveillance. See this manual for disclosure of the pacemaker pulse rejectioncapability of this 
instrument.
Never use the monitor during MRIs or CT scans.
Never use cables with exposed conductors. Only use undamaged cables and connectors to avoid personal 
injury.
Never simultaneously touch the patient and the input or output terminal of the monitor.
The monitor can be used with electrosurgical devices. To avoid burns or death, ensure that the 
electrosurgical circuitry is properly connected.
Ensure that the patient is not connected to any metal, the surface of any conductors, or grounded parts of 
any devices when a defibrillator is in use. Never touch the patient, table, or instruments during 
defibrillation.
Never use the monitor in an environment of anesthetic gases.
Disconnect the AC power supply and remove the battery before disassembling the monitor.
