PM (Preventive Maintenance) Tab: Enter PM Logs
PM Log - Check System Health
Check that there is an acceptable number of pending tasks, for the Archiver, Router and 
Web services. In addition, check that there is an acceptable number of pending actions, 
based on the related tasks (there should be a smaller percentage of actions in comparison 
to the tasks).
An acceptable number of tasks is dependent on workflow and the determination is based 
on site-specific information and common sense. For example, the following factors 
should be considered when determining if a task level seems appropriate:

Number of images being sent in a day

Has the offline sync utility run and found files to synchronize?

Compression schedule - is the system waiting for compression to complete before 
other tasks can complete?

Retry levels? Determine why retries are failing? Are the retries succeeding upon 
retry? Are the retry dates current? or from previous dates?
1.
Click the Archives link to display pending archive-related tasks. Based on the 
current system activity, determine if there is an acceptable number of pending tasks. 
Select the Yes/No radio buttons appropriately.
2.
Click the Router link to display the pending router-related tasks. Based on the 
current system activity, determine if there is an acceptable number of pending tasks. 
Select the Yes/No radio buttons appropriately.
3.
Click the Web link to display the pending web-related tasks. Based on the current 
system activity, determine if there is an acceptable number of pending tasks. Select 
the Yes/No radio buttons appropriately.
4.
Click the Actions link to display the pending actions in the system.  Based on the 
current number of pending tasks, determine if there is an acceptable number of 
pending actions. Select the Yes/No radio buttons appropriately.
5.
When all of the above tasks are complete, select the Checked System Health 
checkbox. 
6.
If necessary, add any additional information in the Comments box.

PM (Preventive Maintenance) Tab: Enter PM Logs
PM Log - Disk Space Management
Click the Disk Space Management link to run the Disk Space Management Status 
utility. 
The Disk Space Management Status (DSM) utility provides a graphical, real-time 
snapshot of the disk space management status. Statistics for the managed disk spaces are 
calculated.
1.
Click the Calculate DSM button to display the DSM status.
2.
When the calculation is complete, each section displays how much space has been 
used in the Total Used Space, Configured Max Size, High Watermark and Low 
Watermark categories:
In addition, the directory path for each managed disk space is shown. Also, a usage bar 
shows the values in a graphical format. Note that this utility may take several minutes to 
process all the information on a large system. 
Check that the used disk space falls between the high and low watermark for the Staging, 
Short-Term Storage and Web locations. 

If the used disk space is below the low watermark, it is very possible that the system 
simply hasn’t reached low watermark level yet.

If the used disk space is above the high watermark, the Disk Space Management 
services may have failed and the system is not being properly monitored. Check error 
logs for Disk Space Management issues.

Based on the information shown by the utility, enter the used space for each 
category and select the appropriate Yes/No radio button based on whether the 
space falls between the watermarks.

Based on the trends shown by the utility, select the appropriate Yes/No radio 
button based on whether it appears that the Archiver and Web services are 
performing correctly.

Click the Number of Files link to display the various long-term storage 
locations. Based on the information shown by this link, select the appropriate 
Yes/No radio button based on whether is appears that the number of files not 
being migrated is acceptable.

If necessary, enter any additional comments in the Comments field.

PM (Preventive Maintenance) Tab: Enter PM Logs
PM Log - Image Vault Services
Click the Image Vault Services link to display the Service Manager utility.
When the utility screen appears, each service is listed, as well as it's current status, such 
as Running, Stopped or Unknown. 

If the services are stopped, check the system logs to determine if the service stopped 
normally or abnormally.

If the service stopped abnormally, attempt to restart the service and restore the 
functionality. 

If the service stopped normally, it was likely stopped by a user for a specific 
reason - attempt to determine this user and the reason before restarting the 
service.

If the services are shown as Unknown, determine if the associated functionality was 
installed or licensed. 

If a service is shown as Running, you have the ability to stop the service by 
clicking the Stop button.

If a service is shown as Stopped, you have the ability to start the service by 
clicking the Start button.

If a service is shown as Unknown, the service should be investigated as to why it 
is appearing on this system.

If  you attempt to change the status of a service by clicking the Start/Stop 
button, click the Refresh button to re-display the services and verify that the 
status is changed.

On the PM Log screen, select the appropriate Yes/No radio button based on whether 
all the necessary Image Vault services are running.

If necessary, enter any additional comments about the findings in the Comments 
box.
PM Log - Collected System Data
To complete this section, you will need to gather information outside of the Service 
Tools interface. Therefore, obtain this information before attempting to complete the PM 
log, since if you exit the log to obtain the information, the log information is not saved.

Check the application logs for errors.

Check the DiskXtender logs (if applicable) for errors.

Check the Plasmon logs (if applicable) for errors.

On the PM Log screen, select the Collected System Data checkbox when all the 
system data has been evaluated..

If necessary, enter any additional comments about the findings in the Comments 
box.

PM (Preventive Maintenance) Tab: Enter PM Logs
PM Log - Validate Database Integrity
1.
Click the Ran IVInteg Utility to check for integrity violation link to display the 
IVInteg utility. 
The IVInteg Utility screen opens, allowing you to run the utility and check the 
subsequent log. See “IVInteg Utility” on page 4-12 for more information on how to 
use this screen.
2.
On the PM Log screen, select the Validated Database Integrity checkbox when all 
the utility has been run and the results evaluated..
3.
If necessary, enter any additional comments about the findings in the Comments 
box.
PM Log - Perform Cleanup Tasks
Click the Cleaned link to display the Clean Temporary Space utility. 
The Clean Temporary Space utility is used to clean (delete) the temporary files location 
used by the Image Vault services.  Note that this utility is also a scheduled task, 
configured to run on a weekly basis. Before running this utility on an ad hoc basis, 
consider the time remaining until the next scheduled run of this utility. 
The current contents of the location are shown in the Current Directory Contents pane 
when this utility option is first selected.

The default file path for the temporary files location is pre-entered in the Temp File 
Path field. If necessary, change this location. You may then need to click Refresh to 
display the most current contents of the directory.

Enter a numeric value in the Days field to delete temporary files that have not been 
accessed in that many days. 

Click the Clean Temp Files button (above the Output Log pane).

When the utility finishes, the output from the utility is then shown in the Output Log 
pane.
This utility only deletes temporary files with the correct file prefixes (files created by the 
Image Vault services).

When the temporary file space is cleaned, select the Performed Cleanup Tasks 
checkbox, as well as the Cleaned temporary file space checkbox.

If necessary, enter any additional comments in the Comments field.

PM Log - Perform Disk Defragmentation
To complete this section, you must run the Disk Defragmenter utility outside the

The Disk Defragmenter option displays the Windows Disk Defragmenter screen. Only 
perform the Defragment portion of this procedure when it appears that system 
performance is compromised by fragmented space.

Select the Disk Defragmenter utility in the Windows 2003 Utilities section.

D) and click Analyze.

Drive defragmentation checkbox, as well as the associated drive radio buttons.

PM (Preventive Maintenance) Tab: Enter PM Logs
PM Log - Verify Backups
There are two types of backups to verify for this section.
The database backup is performed by copying the current database to an secondary 
location. This location is configured in the system backup parameters, so the system 
backup will not run properly if the database is not copied into the location.
The system data backup is a media backup (usually tape) of all data within the User Data 
directory.

To check the database backup, confirm that there is a file with the current date in the 
D:\gehc\Image Vault\User Data\Backup\Current Backup directory.

To check the system data backup, open the file with the most recent date in the 
C:\Documents and Settings\IVService\Local Settings\Application 
Data\Microsoft\Windows NT\NT Backup\Data directory. Confirm that the log 
states that the backup completed and no errors are listed.

After the backups are verified, select the Verified backups are being 
performed checkbox.

In addition, select the checkboxes for each of the backup types and use the 
calendar icons to enter the date for these backups.

If necessary, enter any additional comments in the Comments field.
PM Log - Test SNMP Alert

After the SNMP alert is tested, select the Tested SNMP Alerts mechanism 
checkbox.

In addition, select the Trap sent and received on the RAP checkbox.

If necessary, enter any additional comments in the Comments field.
PM Log - Check OS Patches

Click the Operating System link to display a list of the currently installed Windows 
operating system security patches.

After the patches are confirmed against the list of patches that should be installed, 
select the Operating System patched to latest approved level checkbox.

If necessary, enter any additional comments in the Comments field.
Check the Image Vault 4.2 Pre-Installation Manual (5183693-100) for information on 
what patches should be installed on the system.

Revision 1 
5183865-100
PM (Preventive Maintenance) Tab: Enter PM Logs
PM Log - Check Version Level
To complete this section, the version level must be checked before starting the PM log. 
 This is necessary, because if you exit the log to run the utility, the log information is not 
saved.
On the Home tab, Current System Status pane, confirm that the application software is 
at the appropriate release level.

After the version is verified, select the Application software at the latest approved 
version checkbox.

If necessary, enter any additional comments in the Comments field.
PM Log - Check Media Status for Plasmon Library
Click the Media Status link to connect to the Plasmon interface and check the status of 
the media.
When the interface appears, confirm that no media is in an unreliable or unusable state.

After the media is verified, select the Checked Media Status for Plasmon library if 
it exists checkbox.

If necessary, enter any additional comments in the Comments field.
PM Log - Run Streams Utility for Macintosh Stubs
The Image Vault sites that contain current or historical image data from Macintosh-based 
clients (Vivid 5 scanners) or MODs that contain Macintosh data and are utilizing the 
DiskXtender application to manage a direct-attached library may need to run the Streams 
utility periodically to delete the alternate data streams created by the Macintosh systems.
Note that only systems containing this combination are affected.
The user will notice that the extended drive, managed by the DiskXtender application, 
runs out of available space. Macintosh systems create alternate streams of data on the 
extended drive managed by DiskXtender. However, DiskXtender does not support 
alternate streams of data. The alternate data streams are not purged by DiskXtender and 
use library space.
Run the following utility at least once a month, or whenever it is noticed that the space 
available on the extended drive or library performance is severely impacted. Note that if 
alternate data streams are deleted, they are restored by DiskXtender when the file is 
fetched; therefore, no data is lost through the use of this utility.
1.
Verify the DiskXtender application reports "zero files pending move".

Locate and open the ...\transaction log for DiskXtender.

Stop the DiskXtender application.

Delete all files currently in the ...\transaction log for DiskXtender.

PM Log - Additional Notes
There are three free-format text boxes that allow you to enter additional maintenance 
information.

In the Hardware Components (FRU) replaced or modified box, enter any 
pertinent information about hardware replacements performed since the last PM log 
was entered.

In the Software Updates box, enter pertinent information about any software 
upgrades or patches that were installed since the last PM log was entered.

In the Additional Notes box, enter any other information that could prove useful to 
the next service engineer or the customer.

After all checks are complete in the PM log, review this information with the 
customer if possible. When the customer acknowledges that the maintenance log 
is complete and accurate, select the Reviewed with Customer checkbox.

Enter the site name in the Customer Name field and the current date in the Date 
field.

Click the Save button to save the PM log.
View PM Logs
Click View PM Logs to display a list of all PM logs entered for this system.
Click any of the logs to display the contents of the log. Note, however, that you cannot 
edit or change these logs in any way.

Network Status
The Network Status option displays all current active network connections to the Image 
Vault system. In other words, it displays which applications are listening on which ports. 
In a troubleshooting scenario, be sure to check if port 3100 (the Image Vault system) is 
listed.
The display includes the following information:

Protocol

Local Address

Foreign Address

State (such as Listening)
Scheduled Tasks
The Scheduled Tasks option displays the configuration details about all scheduled tasks 
for this system. The following scheduled tasks should be listed:

Clean Temp Space - IV Service  

Clean Temp Space - Windows Temp  

Database State Update  

IV4 Daily Backup  

Offline Sync
All scheduled tasks should be examined to determine that they are running at their 
appropriate scheduled time and that each task has completed successfully in the last run.
If you click Summary, the following essential information is displayed:

Task Name

Date of Next Scheduled Run

Status
If you click Verbose, the following additional information is displayed: 


Active Database Connections
The Active Database Connections utility allows you to display the current active 
connections to the Image Vault database. This is the same list that can be obtained by 
displaying the active connections through the Image Vault interface.

A list of all currently connected users displays in the lower pane. 

This pane also displays the user ID, the last request time, how the user is connected 
and the node address. 
Use this utility to determine if a necessary connection, such as a specific Ultrasound lab, 
is currently seen as connected to the Image Vault system. If a system is expected to be 
connected and is not, further investigation into other issues, such as IP addressing, may 
be necessary.
Click Refresh to update the display pane and obtain the most current listing.
Audit Log
The View Audit Log utility allows you to view database events, filtered by user-defined 
parameters.
The Audit log shows all user interactions with the database and displays these 
interactions in an user/action/details/timestamp format. The filter capability of the log 
allows you to search for specific events, based on the situation creating the error. For 
example, if the user is requesting information on a patient record that appears to be 
missing, you can search on the Patient ID to determine if the database contains 
information on the patient.
Enter any or all of the following filters to display specified logging events:

Begin Date - use the calendar icon to select the beginning date for the search

End Date - use the calendar icon to select the ending date for the search

Event - enter free-form text to search for a particular event type

Created by - enter free-form text to search for a particular service that generated the 
event

Patient ID - enter a patient ID to be located in the logs

Last Name - enter a patient's last name to be located in the logs
Click Clear if you want to erase all the entered parameters.
Click Refresh to re-display the audit logging.

Backup Logs
The Backup Logs utility displays the log files in the following directory:
C:\Documents and Settings\IVService\Local Settings\Application 
Data\Microsoft\Windows NT\NT Backup\Data 
Logs from the last 10 backups are saved in this directory. Open the latest backup log file 
and confirm that the backup was processed correctly and no errors are listed.
Clean Userdefs
The Clean Userdefs utility restores the default system settings, deleting the user-defined 
settings. This means that all configuration settings established through the interface, as 
well as settings like custom user accounts, will be erased. 
During the initial installation of the Image Vault application, the service engineer is 
requested to document all site-specific configuration settings. In the extreme situation 
where the user definitions are deleted in error, and the settings need to be re-configured, 
the initial settings should be available in this workbook.
CAUTION
This is a very serious action, and should only be taken if you are ABSOLUTELY 
certain that you want to delete all user settings. Be sure that the user definitions 
are saved to a current backup before using this utility.
To use the utility, click the Clean Userdefs button.
Clean Temp Space
The Clean Temporary Space utility is used to clean (delete) the temporary files location 
used by the Image Vault services.  The current contents of the location are shown in the 
Current Directory Contents pane when this utility option is first selected.
1.
The default file path for the temporary files location is pre-entered in the Temp File 
Path field. If necessary, change this location (if a non-standard default location was 
established during the initial installation of the application). You may then need to 
click Refresh to display the most current contents of the directory.
2.
Enter a numeric value in the Days field to delete temporary files that have not been 
accessed in that many days. 
3.
Click the Clean Temp Files button (above the Output Log pane).
4.
The output from the utility is then shown in the Output Log pane.
This utility only deletes temporary files with the correct file prefixes (files created by the 
Image Vault services).

5183865-100
Utilities Tab: Image Vault Utilities
Database State Update
The Database State Update utility is used to synchronize the image file states between 
the short- and long-term storage locations. The utility searches the database records, 
checking for file existence in the both the short- and long-term storage locations. The 
database is then modified based on the file existence in each location. 
Note that this utility is processor intensive and can take several hours to complete on a 
large database. Only run this utility during off-peak hours to minimize impact on users.
1.
To run the utility, click the Start button.
2.
As the utility locates files that must be updated, and then updates the database, log 
entries of this activity are displayed in the lower pane. To refresh this log entry list, 
either click the Refresh button periodically or select the Auto Update checkbox to 
have the system refresh the system at certain intervals.
Disk Space Status (DSM)
The Disk Space Management Status (DSM) utility provides a graphical, real-time 
snapshot of the disk space management status. Statistics for the following managed disk 
spaces are calculated:

Staging Location Space

Short-Term Storage Space

Web Cache Space
Click the Calculate DSM button to display the DSM status.
When the calculation is complete, each section displays how much space has been used 
in each of the following categories:

Total Used Space

Configured Max Size

High Watermark

Low Watermark
The directory path for each managed disk space is shown, and a usage bar shows the 
values in a graphical format. Also note that the values are shown in both MB and GB.

Check that the used disk space falls between the high and low watermark for the 
Staging, Short-Term Storage and Web locations. 

If the used disk space is below the low watermark, it is very possible that the 
system simply hasn’t reached low watermark level yet.

If the used disk space is above the high watermark, the Disk Space Management 
services may have failed and the system is not being properly monitored. Check 
error logs for Disk Space Management issues.
Note that this utility may take several minutes to process all the information on a large 
system.

5183865-100
Utilities Tab: Image Vault Utilities
Expected System Services
The Expected System Services utility displays all services currently installed on the 
system. In addition, the following information is displayed:

Display Name - the name of the service that is displayed on the Services screen

Service Name - the executable name for the service

Status - the current status of the service, either Running or Stopped.
While a service may be installed and is a valid service on the system, it may be set to a 
stopped status by the Image Vault application. See the list below for a list of all services 
that should be running on a fully functioning Image Vault system.

Expected Status - If a service is expected to be on the system, whether it is running 
or not, it appears in the list. If the status is not in the expected state, meaning if it is 
expected to be running, but it is stopped (or vice versa), the service is highlighted in 
orange. This service should be investigated as to how it came to be in an 
unexpected status. 

However, if a service is not expected, but is installed on the system, the service is 
highlighted in yellow. The column will display Unexpected Service. This service 
should be investigated to determine their source and how they came to be 
installed on this system.
Click Refresh to display the most current status of the system services.
IVInteg Utility
The IVInteg utility checks the contents of the database and checks the filesystem to 
confirm matching with the database tables to locate any existing data integrity issues in 
the database.
The analysis report created during this procedure, if issues are found, should be 
forwarded to the Image Vault engineering team for resolution.
On the IVInteg Utility page:

The top half of the screen displays the current status of the utility (running, not 
running) and provides the ability to start the utility. Click Start in the Control 
section to run the "short log" version of the utility. The short log version only collects 
the issues statistics, without acquiring detailed information about the affected exams. 
If you want to run a full log version or want to evaluate the log more thoroughly, 
please refer to Image Vault 4.2 Database Protection Mechanism Tools Manual 
(5184652-100) - available on the Image Vault 4.2 Standard Documentation CD.

The lower half of the screen displays the output log from the utility processing. Note 
that you can either select Refresh to get a more current snapshot as the utility runs, 
or select the Auto Update checkbox to have the system periodically refresh the log 
screen. Also note that only the first 10,000 lines of the log are shown in this window. 
If you need to see the entire log, follow the on-screen link to locate and open the full 
log file.

Utilities Tab: Image Vault Utilities
Check the summary statistics at the bottom of the log to determine if there are currently 
outstanding issues in the database and/or filesystem. If yes, contact the Image Vault 
engineering team. Be prepared to supply the output log from this utility.
NAS Logs
The NAS Logs utility allows you to display the error logs from the Plasmon UDO 
archive appliance. You can also save and print these logs.
1.
Click the Refresh button to retrieve the latest version of the logs from the appliance.
2.
Enter the following:

IP Address - Enter the IP address for the Plasmon UDO archive appliance

Port - Enter port number associated with the Plasmon UDO archive appliance
3.
Click Fetch Logs. When the logs display, you can save the file on the server or send 
the file to print.
Offline Sync
The Offline Synchronization utility is used to regenerate Archiver tasks to move files to 
an Archived state.
The utility searches the database for files that are not in Offline, Nearline, or Archived 
state. If files are found, the task table is searched to determine if there is an outstanding 
task to move this file. If not, a task is generated to move the file to the Archived state.
While this utility can be run on an ad hoc basis, it is also a scheduled task that runs 
nightly. Since this utility is processor intensive, you may want to consider the next 
scheduled time for this utility before starting the utility from this interface.
CAUTION
Note that this utility is processor intensive and can take several hours to 
complete on a large database. Only run this utility during off-peak hours to 
minimize the impact on the users.

To run the utility, click the Start button. You can then exit the utility screen, as this 
does not stop the utility itself from running. When you re-enter the utility screen, the 
status field will display whether the utility is still running or not.

As the utility locates files that must be moved, and then creates the Archiver tasks, 
log entries of this activity are displayed in the lower pane. To refresh this log entry 
list, either click the Refresh button periodically or select the Auto Update checkbox 
to have the system refresh the system at certain intervals.

4-14

5183865-100
Utilities Tab: Image Vault Utilities
Resource File Utility
The Resource File utility allows you to display the target and test root of the resource 
files used in the Image Vault application. 
Note that the target root file for each resource file is the target directory on the C drive, or 
the system default version. The following resource files are available:

globalconfig.res

Phoenix.res

Tasks.res

icon.res

logging.res

daldatabase.res
The test root file is then the delta, or changes, to the target root file implemented by the 
user.

To display either the target or test root files, click the appropriate link next to the 
desired resource file name. Note that this only allows you to display the file, not 
make changes or save the file.

To make changes or save the target or test root files, click the Save link next to the 
desired resource file name. Select one of the following options:

Open it with a default application - selecting this option opens the resource file 
in Notepad.

Open it with... - Click Choose and select an alternate text file option.

Save it to disk - selecting this option allows you to save the resource file to a 
location on the server.

Click OK.
Service Manager
The Service Manager utility allows you to display, in a snapshot form, the status of the 
current Image Vault services. This does NOT include the Windows 2003 utilities.

If the services are stopped, check the system logs to determine if the service stopped 
normally or abnormally.

If the service stopped abnormally, attempt to restart the service and restore the 
functionality. 

If the service stopped normally, it was likely stopped by a user for a specific 
reason - attempt to determine this user and the reason before restarting the 
service.

If the services are shown as Unknown, determine if the associated functionality was 
installed or licensed.

Each service is listed, as well as it's current status, such as Running, Stopped or 
Unknown.

If a service is shown as Running, you have the ability to stop the service by clicking 
the Stop button.

If a service is shown as Stopped, you have the ability to start the service by clicking 
the Start button.

If a service is shown as Unknown, the service should be investigated as to why it is 
appearing on this system.
If  you attempt to change the status of a service by clicking the Start/Stop button, click 
the Refresh button to re-display the services and verify that the status is changed.
Set Debug Utility
The Set Debug utility does not have a valid Image Vault debugging use. 
SQL Query Interface
The SQL Query Interface allows you to enter an SQL command without using the SQL 
application. However, you can only select database tables with this interface. If you need 
to delete or update database tables, you will need to use the actual SQL application.
1.
Enter the desired SQL command in the text box.
2.
Click Execute to process the command.
Task View
The Task View utility allows you to display all the pending tasks in the system, as well 
as filter the tasks by service and task type.
Check that there is an acceptable number of pending tasks, for the Archiver, Router and 
Web services. In addition, check that there is an acceptable number of pending actions, 
based on the related tasks (there should be a smaller percentage of actions in comparision 
to the tasks).
An acceptable number of tasks is dependent on workflow and the determination is based 
on site-specific information and common sense. For example, the following factors 
should be considered when determining if a task level seems appropriate:

Number of images being sent in a day

Has the offline sync utility run and found files to synchronize?

Compression schedule - is the system waiting for compression to complete before 
other tasks can complete?

Retry levels? Determine why retries are failing? Are the retries succeeding upon 
retry? Are the retry dates current? or from previous dates?

Virtual Console Observation
The Virtual Console Observation option allows the Online Center to set the server in a 
state so that remote connectivity can be established.
Click Start to place the system in a ready state. Click Stop when the system no longer 
needs to be accessed remotely.
WARNING
If the Virtual Console Observation is disabled and then re-enabled through the 
Common Service Desktop, and the customer is enabled for remote access, a 
procedure needs to be run again to re-set the registry key. This procedure is 
documented in the Image Vault 4.2 Installation Guide.
iLinq Configuration Utility
The iLinq Configuration utility allows you to configure the system to allow modem dial 
out capability.
If the system is not on a network, and needs a modem to dial out, select the checkbox on 
this utility screen.
Switch Modem to OnNetwork
The Switch Modem to OnNetwork option allows the system to be connected through a 
modem. The option is only available if a modem is connected to the system.
DICOM Verify
The DICOM Verify utility allows you perform a DICOM ping on any DICOM device in 
the network connected to the Image Vault server. This test performs a TCP/IP address 
ping, as well as confirming that the DICOM application is active on the device.
1.
Enter the AE title or the IP address of the device to be pinged.
2.
Click the Verify button.
If the verify results are negative, first determine if the device being pinged is actually a 
DICOM device. 
If yes, then perform a standard network ping on the device (outside of the Service Tools 
interface). If the network ping shows that the TCP/IP address is available, the DICOM 
Verify probably failed because the DICOM application is inactive.

Chapter 1
Introduction to Magnetic Resonance
Imaging
1.1
Introduction
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a medical imaging technique and diagnostic tool in radi-
ology based on Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR). It is capable of visualizing internal struc-
tures of the body in detail, providing information to qualitatively and quantitatively describe
the shape, size, and integrity of gray and white matter structures, as well as other organs.
One may ask: Why do we need MRI scanners when we already have Computed Tomography
(CT) scanners, which produce high-quality images? The answer lies in the essence of medical
image formation and the specific physical principles utilized by MRI.
1.2
Why MRI
The crucial difference between CT and MRI becomes evident when we look at soft tissue
imaging.
Intuition: MRI vs. CT
The Soft Tissue Contrast Advantage
CT is extremely eﬀicient for imaging bones, showing bone details with great clarity.
However, for soft tissues such as:
• Ligaments
• Nerves
• Brain (Gray and White matter differentiation)
• Muscles and Fat
MRI is the optimum choice. MRI provides much higher contrast for these tissues compared
to CT.
Beyond its excellent soft tissue contrast, MRI offers additional unique features:
1. True Multi-planar Imaging: MRI can acquire truly native images in any plane (Axial,
Sagittal, Coronal), while CT mainly acquires axial images and then reconstructs images
in other planes.

1.3
Basic Physics: The Hydrogen Atom
An MRI scanner does not image every element in the body.
It is specialized to image one
particular atom: the hydrogen atom (1H).
1.3.1
Why Hydrogen?
Hydrogen is chosen for two main reasons:
1. Abundance: It is plentiful in living organisms. The human body is composed of 50–65%
water (H2O), and most of the human body is hydrogen.
2. Spin Characteristics: Each hydrogen atom has a single proton in its nucleus. Only
nuclei with an odd number of protons and neutrons have a net spin. Since hydrogen has
only one proton, it possesses a powerful magnetic moment essential for producing the NMR
signal.
1.3.2
Spinning: The Proton as a Magnet
The atomic nucleus is the small, dense region consisting of protons and neutrons at the center
of an atom. A hydrogen atom consists of a nucleus containing a single positively charged proton
with a single negative electron orbiting it. The key physical concept here is spin.
Spin is a fundamental quantum mechanical property, representing intrinsic angular momen-
tum. While it is often visualized as a physical rotation (like a planet rotating on its axis), it is
actually an intrinsic property of the particle itself, similar to mass or charge.

Chapter 1. Introduction to Magnetic Resonance Imaging
8
Physics Principle: The Classical Model vs. Quantum Reality
The Classical Model: To make MRI easier to understand, we visualize the proton as a
positively charged sphere spinning on its axis. According to Faraday’s Law of Induction,
a moving charge creates a magnetic field.
Therefore, we treat the proton as a ”tiny
magnet” (dipole) with North and South poles.
The Quantum Reality: The proton has a magnetic dipole moment µ not because it is
physically spinning, but because of its intrinsic quantum state.
In the absence of an external magnetic field, the directions of these tiny magnets are entirely
random. This results in zero net magnetization (M = 0).
1.4
Behavior in a Magnetic Field (B0)
When a person is placed inside an MRI scanner, they are exposed to a very strong, uniform
external magnetic field, denoted as B0. This field is produced by the scanner’s main magnet
(typically 1.5T to 11T, compared to the Earth’s magnetic field of approx. 60 µT).
Under the influence of B0, the protons do not all align perfectly, but their orientations
become restricted to two quantum states:
1. Parallel: Aligned with the magnetic field lines (Low energy state).
2. Anti-parallel: Opposite to the direction of the magnetic field (High energy state).
1.4.1
Net Magnetization and the Boltzmann Equation
Is the net magnetization still zero? No. However, the difference in population between these two
states is not a fixed constant; it is governed by the Boltzmann Distribution. This distribution
depends on the temperature of the tissue and the strength of the magnetic field:

N↑

(1.1)
Field Strength and the ”Excess” Protons
Because ∆E is proportional to B0, the number of excess protons in the parallel state
increases as the magnet gets stronger:
• At 1.5T, the excess is approximately 3 per million.
• At 3.0T, the excess is approximately 6 per million.
While these numbers seem small, the vast number of protons in the human body (approx.
1019 per mm3 of water) ensures that this tiny ratio creates a signal large enough to
measure.

Advanced Physics: The Quantum View of NMR
While classical physics describes precession well, the behavior of hydrogen nuclei can also be
described using quantum mechanics.
1.6.1
Spin States and Energy Levels
The spin of 1H is equal to 1
2.
It can only have two possible measurable states (parallel or
anti-parallel to B0).
• A spin is at its lowest energy when aligned with B0.
• A spin is at its highest energy when opposite to B0.
Without B0, these states are indistinguishable. However, the application of B0 creates an energy
gap, known as the Zeeman Effect.

1.6.2
Zeeman Effect and Energy Transfer
The energy difference (∆E) between the two nuclear spin states is given by:
∆E = γ h
2πB0 = hfL
(1.6)
where h is Planck’s constant.
This relation confirms the Planck-Einstein relation (∆E = hf).
It implies that energy
transfer is quantized. For a spin to flip from low energy to high energy, it must absorb a
photon with energy exactly equal to hfL. This explains why magnetic resonance absorption
only occurs at the specific Larmor frequency.

1.7
Resonance and Excitation
What does Resonance mean? For energy to be eﬀiciently transferred from a source to a receiver,
the frequency of the source must match that of the receiver.
The Swing Analogy
If you want to push a swing and make it go higher, you must push it at the same frequency
as the swing’s natural oscillation.
• If you push randomly (frequency mismatch), the motion dies down.
• If you push at exactly the same frequency (Resonance), energy transfers eﬀiciently,
and the swing oscillates with a larger amplitude.
1.7.1
Phase Coherence: The Hidden Requirement
Energy absorption is only half the story. Before the RF pulse, the protons are precessing at the
Larmor frequency, but they are out of phase (pointing in random directions around the z-axis).
The RF pulse performs two tasks:
1. Energy Transfer: It flips the Net Magnetization (M) from the longitudinal axis (Z)
toward the transverse plane (XY).
2. Phase Coherence: It forces the magnetic moments of the individual protons to move in
sync (in step) with each other.
Crucial Concept: An MRI signal is only generated when the protons possess Phase
Coherence.
Without this synchronization, the individual magnetic moments would cancel
each other out in the transverse plane, resulting in zero signal.

1.10
Advantages
• Non-invasive: Does not use ionizing radiation (unlike CT or X-ray).
• High Contrast: Provides clear visualization and superior differentiation between soft
tissues (e.g., gray vs. white matter, tumor vs. healthy tissue).
• 3D Acquisition: True multi-planar imaging (Axial, Sagittal, Coronal) without moving
the patient.
• Functional Imaging: Can assess physiological states (e.g., fMRI for brain activity, Dif-
fusion Weighted Imaging).
• Safe Contrast Agents: Gadolinium-based agents generally have fewer side effects than
iodinated CT contrast.
1.11
Disadvantages
• Cost: Systems are expensive to purchase, maintain, and operate.
• Scan Time: Long acquisition times (20 to 90 minutes), requiring the patient to remain
perfectly still to avoid motion artifacts.
• Safety Hazards: The powerful magnet acts as a trap for ferromagnetic objects (projectile
effect). It is contraindicated for patients with pacemakers, cochlear implants, or certain
metallic clips.
• Patient Comfort: The bore is narrow (claustrophobia) and the gradient coils produce
loud acoustic noise (up to 120 dB) during scanning.

The Fourier Transform: The Mathematical Engine of MRI
There would be no magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without Fourier Transforms. All image
calculations, signal processing, and image formation in MRI fundamentally rely on the principles
and equations of Fourier analysis.
2.1.1
Understanding the Signal
At the beginning, any source of signal (such as a dynamo or proton), when it rotates, generates
a signal known as a Sine Wave. What distinguishes one signal from another?
1. Amplitude: The strength of the signal.
2. Frequency: The speed at which the source rotates.
Fourier Principle
The Fourier principle states that any complex signal, regardless of its shape, can be
represented as a sum of Sine and Cosine waves with varying frequencies and amplitudes.
Time Domain vs. Frequency Domain
We can represent a signal in two different ways:
• Time Domain: Plotting the signal as a function of time (with the time axis t). The
signal appears as a wave that oscillates and changes over time.
• Frequency Domain: Expressing the signal as a spike at a specific frequency. The height
of the spike represents the amplitude, and its position on the axis represents the frequency.

Chapter 2. Signal Processing, Spatial Encoding, and Image Formation
17
Analogy: The Classroom
Imagine entering a classroom where all the students are talking at once and recording the
sound; you will hear unintelligible noise (a complex signal in the time domain). If you
process this recording through a ”Fourier Analysis,” the analysis will tell you:
• Mohamed speaks at a certain frequency (and certain amplitude).
• Sherif sings at another frequency.
• Ibrahim shouts at yet another frequency.
This is the job of the Fourier Transform: breaking a complex signal down into its basic
Sine wave components.
2.2
Spatial Encoding: Locating the Signal
The main problem: When a patient is placed inside the magnet (B0) and an RF pulse is applied,
the entire body responds in resonance and produces signals at the same frequency. How can we
distinguish the location of each signal to form a sectional image? The solution lies in the use of
Gradients.
The MRI scanner typically has three gradient coils that produce magnetic fields varying
linearly along the three orthogonal axes (X, Y, Z). These gradients are added to B0 but are
much weaker (typically in the range of mT/m).
Figure 2.1: MRI scanner gradients configuration.
2.2.1
Slice Selection (Selecting a Limited Volume)
To image just a single slice (rather than the whole body), the scanner uses several steps:
1. We define a coordinate system where the z-axis is perpendicular to the slice.
2. A Slice Selection Gradient (Gz) is applied.
This creates a magnetic field B(z) =
B0 + zGz.
3. According to the Larmor equation, the frequency becomes dependent on position: f(z) =
fL + γzGz.

2.2.2
The Voxel Concept
After selecting the slice, it is divided into a matrix.
• Pixel: The smallest element of a 2D image.
• Voxel (Volumetric Pixel): Similar to a pixel, but with a thickness equal to the slice
thickness, representing a tiny volume in 3D space.
We read the MR signal coming from each voxel.
2.3
Encoding Within the Slice
After selecting a slice, we still need to localize signals within the plane (differentiating left-right
and top-bottom).
2.3.1
Frequency Encoding (Columns)
We differentiate columns using a Frequency Encoding Gradient (Gf or Gx).
• This gradient is activated during signal readout.
• It creates a field B(x) = B0 + xGf, so each column of voxels precesses at a distinct
frequency f(x) = fL + γxGf.
• Using the Fourier Transform, we can separate these frequencies and therefore localize each
column.
Figure 2.3: Frequency encoding separates signals along one axis.
2.3.2
Phase Encoding (Rows)
This step is trickier. We cannot simply apply another frequency gradient in the orthogonal
direction simultaneously. Instead, we use a Phase Encoding Gradient (Gp or Gy).

content:
Chapter 2. Signal Processing, Spatial Encoding, and Image Formation
20
The Clock Analogy
Imagine a row of clocks, all starting at 12:00.
1. When we turn on the Phase Encoding Gradient, the magnetic field becomes stronger
on one side and weaker on the other.
2. Clocks in the stronger field run faster; clocks in the weaker field run slower.
3. After a short time, we turn off the gradient. The clocks revert to the same speed,
but they now show different times (they have different phases).
4. The clock at the top might read 12:15, the middle 12:00, and the bottom 11:45.
By looking at the ”time” (phase) on the clock, we can determine its physical position
along that axis.
In MRI:
1. The Phase Encoding Gradient is turned on briefly (τ) before signal readout.
2. This creates a phase shift ∆ϕ(y) = γyGpτ along the y-direction.
3. The process is repeated for every line of k-space (every TR), with a different gradient
strength each time.
Figure 2.4: Phase encoding introduces a phase shift along the Y-axis.

Image Reconstruction and k-space
The raw data collected by the MRI scanner is stored in a matrix called k-space.
2.4.1
k-space
Common Misconception
A single point in k-space does not represent a single pixel in the image. Each point in
k-space actually contains information from every voxel within the slice.

K-space exhibits a unique mathematical property called Conjugate Symmetry. Data points

Chapter 3

Weighting
3.1
The Concept of Image Contrast
In the previous lesson, we learned how to reconstruct an image. However, if we simply generated
an image based on the maximum possible signal strength, the image would appear completely
white or ”burned out.” The medical goal is not to obtain the strongest signal, but rather to
achieve contrast.
Definition: Contrast
Contrast is the difference in grayscale (signal intensity) between different tissues. For
example, we do not want the liver and kidney to appear the same shade. We want to
distinguish between them and also between healthy tissues and tumors.
We cannot simply instruct the liver to appear ”white” or the kidney to appear ”black.”
Instead, we use certain physical properties within tissues to manipulate the signal and produce
the desired image contrast.
Figure 3.1: Examples of image contrast. Tissues have different signal intensities depending on
the acquisition parameters.

Determinants of MR Signal
The MR signal emitted from any voxel depends on two main types of factors:

Chapter 4
Pulse Sequences: Gradient Echo and
Spin Echo
4.1
The Challenge of Signal Readout
In the previous chapters, we learned how to use gradients for spatial encoding—to determine
where a signal comes from. However, a practical problem arises during signal acquisition: When
we activate the Frequency Encoding Gradient (Readout Gradient) to read the MR signal,
this very gradient also causes rapid signal loss—destroying the signal before it can be measured!
4.1.1
The Dephasing Problem
Within a single voxel, there are millions of protons. Ideally, all protons within the voxel precess
with the same frequency and phase (they are in-phase). When the readout gradient is applied:
1. The magnetic field strength varies gradually across the voxel.
2. Protons at one end of the voxel precess at a different speed than those at the opposite end.
3. This difference in frequency leads to a loss of phase synchrony (Dephasing), causing very
rapid signal decay. The net signal can drop to zero before there’s a chance to record it.
4.2
Gradient Echo (GRE) Sequence
How do we solve the dephasing problem caused by the readout gradient? Use the gradient itself!
Photon Analogy: Bipolar Gradients
Imagine two photons initially in phase.
1. Dephasing: A gradient causes one photon to speed up, making them out of phase
(signal loss).
2. Reverse Gradient: A negative gradient slows the faster photon, driving the pho-
tons back toward in phase.
3. Readout: The positive gradient is applied to acquire the signal.
4. Echo: Midway through readout, the photons are fully in phase (maximum signal).
32

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p33_c36
content:
Chapter 4. Pulse Sequences: Gradient Echo and Spin Echo
33
This signal that “died” and then “came back to life” is called an Echo. Since we used a
gradient to create it, it is called a Gradient Echo.
Gradient Echo Sequence Diagram
The Gradient Echo (GRE) sequence consists of:
• RF Excitation: The excitation flip angle (α) is often less than 90◦(for example
45◦or 30◦), allowing for faster imaging.
• Frequency Encoding Gradient: This has two distinct parts called “lobes”:
– A negative lobe (dephasing/pre-phasing lobe)
– A positive lobe (readout lobe)
• The area under the negative lobe should be half the area under the positive lobe,
so that the echo occurs at the center of the readout period (TE).
4.2.1
The Ernst Angle
In Gradient Echo sequences, we use low flip angles to allow for very short Repetition Times
(TR). If we used a 90◦pulse with a short TR, the longitudinal magnetization would never have
time to recover, leading to ”saturation” and zero signal. The optimal flip angle that produces
the maximum signal for a given TR and T1 is called the Ernst Angle (αE), defined by:
cos(αE) = e−TR/T1
By using the Ernst Angle, we can scan much faster than Spin Echo sequences while maintaining
a usable Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR).
4.2.2
Spoiled vs. Steady-State GRE
Because GRE sequences use very short TR, the transverse magnetization (Mxy) may not have
fully decayed before the next RF pulse begins.
• Spoiled GRE (e.g., FLASH, T1-FFE): We use extra gradient pulses or RF phase
shifting to ”destroy” the residual transverse magnetization.
This results in pure T1-
weighting.
• Steady-State GRE (e.g., TrueFISP, bSSFP): We ”rewind” the gradients to preserve
the residual magnetization. This creates a complex contrast based on the T2/T1 ratio,
commonly used in cardiac and fetal imaging.
4.3
T2* Decay and Magnetic Field Inhomogeneity
Although Gradient Echo successfully corrects dephasing caused by the readout gradient, it
cannot correct dephasing due to inhomogeneities in the main magnetic field (B0 Inhomogeneity).
4.3.1
What is T2*?
In reality, the main magnetic field is never perfectly homogeneous.
There are always tiny
imperfections or variations in the field that cause some protons to precess slightly faster or

slower than others. This leads to a much faster signal decay than the tissue’s natural T2 decay.
This rapid decay is called T ∗
2 decay (T ∗
2 ≤T2).
Gradient Echo sequences do not compensate for T ∗
2 . As a result, the images produced are
highly sensitive to magnetic field imperfections, which can result in dark areas (artifacts)
at air-bone interfaces or regions with field inhomogeneity.
4.4
Spin Echo (SE) Sequence
To overcome the limitations of T ∗
2 and measure the true tissue T2, the Spin Echo sequence is
used.
4.4.1
The 180-Degree Refocusing Pulse
The key idea is to use an extra radiofrequency (RF) pulse with a 180◦flip angle.
The Car Analogy: The 180 Turn (The Mirror)
Imagine a race where a fast car is far ahead of a slow car (representing dephasing due to
T ∗
2 effects).
1. At time TE/2, a 180◦pulse is applied.
2. The Effect: This pulse acts like a mirror, flipping the racers. The fast car, which
was ahead, is now in the back, while the slow car is now in the front.
3. Rephasing: Because the fast car is still faster, it begins to catch up with the slow
car.
4. The Echo: After another equal time interval (TE/2), the fast car has caught up
with the slow car right at the starting line.
At this instant, the signal reappears strongly, and the effects of magnetic field inhomogeneity
have been canceled out. This is the Spin Echo.
Figure 4.1: Diagram of Spin Echo formation using a 180◦refocusing pulse.

• Only the peak of the echo falls on the true T2 decay curve.
• This technique (Turbo Spin Echo or Fast Spin Echo) significantly speeds up acquisition.

An MRI system contains three major components, each of which is usually in a separate room

you take the covers off, most of the similarities end. The principal components of an MRI system

1. The Magnet: The heart of the MRI system, responsible for creating the main mag-
netic field (B0). Its types, technology, intrinsic design, and field quality are discussed in
Section 5.2.2.
2. RF Transmission System: Generates and transmits radiofrequency (RF) pulses respon-
sible for excitation.
3. Gradient System: Produces magnetic field gradients (gradient pulses) for spatial encod-
ing of the image.
4. RF Receiving System: Receives the weak signals emitted from the patient, amplifies
them, and converts them from analog to digital form.
5. Image Reconstruction System (Array Processor): Handles the complex mathemat-
ical operations (such as Fourier Transform) to convert digital signals into an image.
6. Host Computer (Main PC): The ”maestro” that coordinates and manages all the other
systems, gathers results, and serves as the main user interface for the technician.
5.1.1
MRI Suite Layout and RF Shielding (Faraday Cage)
The components of a complete MR system are usually located in three adjacent rooms: the
Magnet Room, Equipment Room, and Control Room. The MRI scan room is not an ordinary
room; it must be electrically and magnetically shielded from the outside world.

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p39_c43
content:
Chapter 5. MRI System Hardware: The Magnet and Architecture
39
RF Shielding Requirements
All walls of the magnet room must be completely covered with a conductive material such
as copper or steel, creating a Faraday cage.
• Purpose: Prevent strong RF signals generated inside the room from leaking out and
interfering with external equipment.
• Prevent any external radiofrequency (RF) waves (such as FM radio, television sig-
nals, or mobile phones) from penetrating into the MRI room and interfering with
the scan.
If external RF waves enter, the MRI system may detect them as if they came from
the patient, resulting in image artifacts and distortion. To achieve this, the room (floor,
ceiling, walls) is lined with copper or aluminum panels, and all cables pass through special
filters to ensure signal purity.
Magnet Room
This room contains the MR magnet, its shell/enclosure, support footings, and patient table.
Cables, vents, and wiring usually enter the top of the magnet assembly passed along a tray
in the ceiling. Some wires and tubing may pass from below along trenches in the floor. The
walls perform several independent functions: magnetic shielding to confine the fringe field;
acoustic shielding to restrict noise transmission to the control room and beyond; radio-frequency
shielding. The floor must be able to support the considerable weight of the magnet (e.g., 10,000
lbs for a 1.5 T scanner). Finishings typically contain closets or storage areas for MR accessories,
phantoms, and patient support items. A sink, oxygen, and suction equipment are also generally
needed. Adjustable lighting (direct current, LED or short filament bulbs) is advised to avoid
vibration and RF interference. A window with a remote video monitoring system is often present
to view the patient.

(b) RF room containing the magnet and patient ta-
ble.

5.2
Main Components of the MRI System
5.2.1
The Gantry and its Subassemblies
The gantry of an MRI system can be intimidating due to its size, especially once the patient is
positioned. It contains the main magnet and several other electromagnetic devices essential to
producing MR images. The gantry of a superconducting MRI system is considered to have three
main subassemblies: the patient couch, the primary electromagnet assembly, and the various
secondary electromagnets.
Patient Table (Couch)
The patient couch performs the two functions of support and position. It should, at a minimum,
be able to accept patients weighing up to 150 kg (∼330 lb) at near floor level and raise the patient
with power assist to the level of the gantry patient aperture. From this position outside the
gantry, the couch should be capable of moving to the imaging position under power assist to
within ±1 mm. This precision is obtained with specialty gears and electronic registers; each
revolution of the smallest drive gear corresponds to a 1 mm movement.

The magnet is the most expensive and complex component in the MRI system. Magnets are
categorized by their shape and by their method of generating the main magnetic field.
Classification by Shape
• Open Magnet: Composed of two large disks (top and bottom) with the patient positioned
in between.
– Advantages: More comfortable for the patient (reduces claustrophobia), allows an
attendant to be present.
– Disadvantages: Lower field strength (often less than 0.5 Tesla), resulting in lower
image quality (low SNR). More sensitive to temperature changes and external inter-
ference.
• Closed Magnet (Tunnel): Consists of a tunnel in which the patient enters.
– Advantages: High magnetic field strength (1.5–7 Tesla or more), superior image
quality, and faster scanning.
– Disadvantages: Can cause discomfort or claustrophobia for some patients, and is
more expensive.

A. Permanent Magnet
These systems use large blocks of magnetized iron, similar to con-
ventional permanent magnets.
• Design: Two large disks of magnetic materials surrounded by a massive iron yoke, which
can weigh up to 15 tons.
• Thermal Stability: The magnetic field changes with temperature, requiring precise
temperature control (not exceeding 0.01◦C fluctuation). Loss of air conditioning can lead
to days of instability.

content:
Chapter 5. MRI System Hardware: The Magnet and Architecture
45
• Safety: The magnetic field is always present and cannot be turned off. Ferromagnetic
objects require significant force to remove if stuck.
B. Resistive Magnet
This type operates using the concept of an electromagnet—a copper
coil through which electric current passes.
• Operating Principle: Very high current (e.g., 170 Amperes for 0.2 Tesla) is passed
through coils with electrical resistance.
• Major Drawback: Resistance generates tremendous heat (P = I2R), requiring large
chillers and consuming a great deal of electricity. Production has nearly stopped due to
high operating costs and thermal management.
• Advantage: Can be turned off in emergency cases.
C. Superconducting Magnet
This is the modern technology standard for MRI, designed to
generate high magnetic fields (1.5 Tesla and above) without excess heat and continuous power
consumption by eliminating resistance.
Superconductivity Principle
A wire made of a special alloy (e.g., Niobium-Titanium) is used. When cooled to near
absolute zero (4 Kelvin or −269◦C) with liquid helium, its resistance becomes zero.
• Ramping (Initial): Electric current is injected only once at installation to estab-
lish the field. The detailed process is described in Chapter 6.
• Since resistance is zero, the current circulates indefinitely without further external
power.
• This design produces a highly stable and strong magnetic field.
Advanced Magnet Design Features (Intrinsic to Hardware)
• Homogeneity: To obtain accurate images, the magnetic field must be extremely uniform
within the imaging volume (DSV). Superconducting magnet windings are divided into
segments with calculated gaps to create a ”homogeneous sphere” (typically 50 cm diameter)
at the isocenter. Further field correction (shimming) is discussed in Section 5.2.3.
• Active Shielding: High magnetic fields extend outward from the scanner (fringe field).
Active shielding uses additional coils wound around the primary coils with current flowing
in the opposite direction. This produces a counter magnetic field that cancels the original
field outside the scanner, maintaining a strong field inside and reducing the 5-Gauss safety
boundary.
• External Interference Shield (EIS): A special short-circuited coil that, according to
the law of induction, generates an opposing field when a large iron object moves nearby.
This cancels out external magnetic disturbances, preserving image stability.
5.2.3
Shimming: Achieving Field Homogeneity
To obtain distortion-free MRI images, the main magnetic field (B0) must be extremely uniform
(homogeneous) within the imaging volume (also called the DSV – Diameter Sphere Volume).
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p46_c52
content:
Chapter 5. MRI System Hardware: The Magnet and Architecture
46
Shimming is the process of correcting any inhomogeneity in the magnetic field. There are two
main categories of shimming:
1. Passive Shimming
Passive shimming aims to correct field inhomogeneities resulting from the local environment
around the MRI scanner (such as steel in the building, support beams, or nearby devices). This
procedure is generally performed once, during installation.
Steps of Passive Shimming:
1. Field Mapping: A special device (Shim Camera or Mapping Device) containing precise
sensors arranged along a semicircle is rotated 360◦to map the magnetic field.
2. Calculation: A computer analyzes the field map and identifies regions of inhomogeneity.
3. Implementation:
• For closed-bore magnets: Long plastic trays are pulled out from inside the magnet,
and small iron pieces (shims/plates) are installed in specifically determined locations
and shapes.
• For open magnets: Small permanent magnets are attached at precise locations on the
magnet poles.
4. Iteration: The field is measured again. If required homogeneity is not met, the shims are
removed and reconfigured as needed. This process may be repeated 3-4 times (iterations)
and can take up to a whole day.
Site Sensitivity
The passive shimming process is highly sensitive to the location. If the magnet is gotten
environmental changes, the process must be restarted from scratch.
2. Active Shimming
When a patient enters the scanner, their own body (because of its magnetic susceptibility) creates
additional inhomogeneity in the magnetic field. This effect varies from patient to patient. For
this reason, active (dynamic) shimming is needed and is tuned for each scan.
Correcting Linear Inhomogeneity (First Order)
If the inhomogeneity is linear (for ex-
ample, a linear gradient in the X, Y , or Z direction):
• The solution already exists: the gradient coils (introduced in Section 5.3).
• By supplying a steady direct current (DC offset) into the gradient coils during the scan,
these coils produce a compensating field that negates the unwanted linear slope created
by the patient.
Correcting High-Order Inhomogeneity (Second Order and Higher)
If the field inho-
mogeneity is more complex (e.g., quadratic curves or higher orders):
• Linear gradient coils are not suﬀicient to correct these distortions.
• Special shim coils, built into the MRI system, are used to generate more complex corrective
fields to cancel such inhomogeneities. (These special coils are sometimes an optional feature
in advanced MRI systems, used in spectroscopy and similar applications.)
Fundamentals of MRI

5.3
Gradient Coils
Gradient coils are located inside the magnet bore, close to the patient, and operate at room
temperature.
They generate linear magnetic field gradients superimposed on the main field
(B0), producing small spatial variations in proton precession frequency or phase that enable
spatial encoding. These coils are also used in active shimming as discussed in Section 5.2.3.
A gradient system consists of three orthogonal coils (x, y, and z), which are rapidly switched on
and off on the order of milliseconds.
The rapid switching of high currents in the presence of the strong B0 field produces Lorentz
forces, causing mechanical vibrations that are responsible for the characteristic acoustic noise
during MRI scans.

5.4
RF Coils
RF coils are used for transmitting and receiving radiofrequency pulses, producing a magnetic
field perpendicular to the primary magnetic field (B0) and oscillating at the resonant frequency
of hydrogen. The RF coil is often referred to as the ”integrated body coil” and is a separate,
removable assembly kept at room temperature. To maximize the signal, coils are placed as close
to the imaged part as possible.
5.4.1
Types of RF Coils
• Body Coil: Built into the scanner, a permanent part for transmitting and receiving.
Used to image large parts of the body.
• Head Coil: Often incorporated into a helmet, used for head scans.
• Surface (or Local) Coils: Placed directly on the area of interest (e.g., knee, spine) to
improve signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Typically receive-only due to inhomogeneous fields.
• Phased Array Coils: Multiple coil elements that receive signals individually, combined
to improve SNR and wide area coverage. Can be transmit or receive.
• Volume Coils (e.g., Birdcage Coil, TEM Coil): Generate a highly uniform B1 field
through quadrature excitation strategies. TEM coils are an alternative for ultra-high field
MRI.

for processing. The evolution of the receiver architecture from analog to digital is one of the
most significant advances in modern MRI.
The Analog-to-Digital Shift
The detected MR signal is an analog wave containing a carrier wave centered at the Larmor
frequency, with imaging information (position and intensity) modulated onto it. The receiver
chain must extract this information with minimal noise addition.
Figure 5.14: Legacy Superheterodyne Receiver Architecture. In older systems, the high-
frequency RF signal was first converted to a lower Intermediate Frequency (IF) using analog
mixers (down-conversion). This complexity required multiple bulky filters (e.g., SAW filters)
and mixers before the signal could be digitized by the Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) and
processed by the Digital Signal Processor (DSP). This architecture is sensitive to image frequency
interference.
1. Coil Decoupling: During the transmission of the high-power RF pulse (up to 10 kW),
the receiver coils (tuned to the same frequency) must be electronically ”detuned” or de-
coupled to prevent them and their sensitive preamplifiers from being burned out.
2. Preamplification: The incoming MR signal is minuscule (on the order of microvolts or
millivolts). It is immediately amplified close to the coil by a Low-Noise Preamplifier
(LNP). Minimizing the distance between the coil and the LNP is critical to prevent
contamination by environmental noise.
3. Digital Conversion (ADC): This is the crucial stage where the signal is converted from
a continuous analog wave to a discrete digital bitstream.
• Legacy Systems: Amplified analog signal was sent via long, shielded copper ca-
bles to the equipment room, where it was digitized after a down-conversion stage
(Superheterodyne architecture).
• Modern Digital Architecture: The newest systems utilize compact, low-power
Analog-to-Digital Converters (ADCs) in close proximity to the coils (often in-
tegrated into the coil housing itself). The digitized data is then sent to the equipment
room via fiber-optic cables.

content:
Chapter 5. MRI System Hardware: The Magnet and Architecture
50
Direct Digital Sampling
Advances in cellular communication technology have enabled the use of high-frequency,
wide-dynamic-range ADCs capable of sampling the MR signal directly at the Larmor
frequency (∼100 MHz). This Direct Digital Sampling eliminates the need for complex
analog frequency down-conversion stages, drastically simplifying the RF front-end and
improving signal fidelity.
Figure 5.15: Direct Conversion (Zero-IF) Receiver Architecture. Modern systems aim
for this architecture, where the RF signal is mixed directly with the Local Oscillator (LO)
to generate the Baseband signal (IF = 0).
This eliminates the complex IF filters required
by the Superheterodyne model. Crucially, in modern MRI, the high-speed ADC can digitize
this baseband I and Q data immediately, allowing the majority of processing (filtering and
demodulation) to be handled entirely in the DSP software.
Demodulation and Quadrature Detection
After digitization, the signal still needs to be decoded.
• Demodulation: This process extracts the embedded imaging information from the carrier
wave by mixing the MR signal with a clean copy of the Larmor frequency carrier (provided
by the RF synthesizer).
• Quadrature Detection (I and Q Channels): The demodulating circuitry is designed
to produce two separate channels, referred to as In-phase (I) and Quadrature (Q).
These two channels represent the real and imaginary components of the transverse mag-
netization, carrying all the necessary information for Fourier transformation and image
reconstruction. Low-pass filters are used to remove the remaining high-frequency carrier
wave components.
Transmit-Receive (T/R) Coils
When the same coil is used for both transmission (sending the RF pulse) and reception (receiving
the MR signal), additional hardware is required:

content:
Chapter 5. MRI System Hardware: The Magnet and Architecture
51
• Hybrid Coupler: Used to distribute the input power equally among multiple transmit
coil elements.
• Transmit-Receive (T/R) Switch: A high-speed electronic switch that directs high-
power energy to the coil during transmission, and then immediately directs the weak
signal toward the LNP and receiver chain during reception. This protects the sensitive
receiver electronics from burnout.
5.4.3
Solid State RF Amplifiers (SSA)
A Solid State Amplifier (SSA) is the modern technology used to generate the high-power ra-
diofrequency (RF) pulses necessary for magnetic resonance excitation. It has virtually replaced
older vacuum tube (Klystron or Magnetron) technology in clinical MRI systems.
SSA: The Modern RF Power Source
Solid State Amplifiers (SSAs) use arrays of power transistors—most commonly LD-
MOS (Laterally Diffused Metal Oxide Semiconductor) devices—to generate and amplify
the RF signal.
Advantages over Vacuum Tubes
The transition to SSA represents a major hardware evolution, offering significant operational
benefits:
• No Warm-up Time: SSAs are ready to operate instantly, unlike vacuum tubes which
require minutes of warm-up time.
• Graceless Failure: If one transistor module fails, the amplifier’s power slightly drops,
but the system remains operational. A vacuum tube fails abruptly, leading to immediate
system downtime.
• Precise Control: SSAs allow for much finer and faster control over the RF pulse shape
and phase. This precision is essential for modern pulse sequences like advanced fat satu-
ration and sophisticated B1 shimming.
• Longevity and Eﬀiciency: SSAs have a longer lifespan, are more energy-eﬀicient, and
generate less waste heat compared to their vacuum tube predecessors.
Architecture: Modular Design
Modern high-power SSAs (which can output up to 35 kW or more) are not single units. They are
built as arrays of multiple smaller modules (e.g., dozens of 1 kW modules) combined in parallel.
This modular design is the core of their reliability and flexibility.
5.5
System Electronics and Control Unit
The MRI system electronics include a powerful and fast signal acquisition computer, radio
frequency amplifiers, gradient power supplies, frequency synthesizers, a pulse sequencing system,
and digital image processing systems. These components are often located in an adjacent, air-
conditioned equipment room. The control unit includes the monitoring screens, keyboard, and
main computer for data processing. The GPU-based reconstruction servers (array processor)

of the operating console often resembles CT or nuclear medicine consoles, with similar controls
but different functions.
5.6
Magnet Supervision: Vital Signs of the MRI
Just as a patient in intensive care needs constant monitoring of vital signs, a superconducting
magnet needs a Magnet Supervision Unit to monitor its status 24 hours a day.
The most
important parameters monitored are:
1. Magnet Pressure: The pressure of helium gas inside the vessel. Any sudden increase or
decrease is a warning sign.
2. Shield Temperatures: The temperatures of the thermal shields (20K and 80K), which
are cooled by the Cold Head.
3. Helium Level: The level of liquid helium.
5.6.1
Measuring Helium Level (The Superconducting Probe)
How can we measure the level of liquid inside a completely sealed vessel filled with strong electric
currents and a powerful magnetic field? We use a probe made of superconductive material.
• The part immersed in the liquid at (4K) has zero resistance.
• The portion above the surface (in helium gas) also has zero resistance, since the gas is still
very cold.
• Problem: If we measure the resistance at this point, it will be zero everywhere, making
it impossible to determine the liquid surface position!
The Measurement Trick: The Heater Pulse
1. A small heater is attached to the probe.
2. A short heat pulse is sent to warm up the wire, causing it to temporarily transition
to its normal (resistive) state.
3. The heater is immediately switched off.
4. Result: The immersed part of the probe cools rapidly and returns to the supercon-
ducting state. The part exposed to the gas remains hot (and resistive) for a longer
time.
5. At this moment, the resistance is measured. The resulting resistance is directly
proportional to the length of the probe exposed to the gas, from which the helium
level can be accurately determined.

Chapter 6
Advanced Magnet Operations:
Cooling, Ramping, and Safety
6.1
Cooling System and Cryogenics
Superconducting magnets require coils to be maintained at a super-cooled, cryogenic state.
Cryogens are liquefied gases (primarily liquid helium) that produce supercold temperatures near
absolute zero. The cooling system includes a cryocooler compressor (high-pressure helium gas
”helium pump”) that circulates liquid helium, and a heat exchanger (or ”chiller”) that pumps
an antifreeze-water mixture to cool the gradients and remove heat from the helium system.
6.1.1
Cryogenics: The 4 Kelvin Environment
As discussed in Chapter 5, for a superconducting magnet to function, its windings must be
cooled to a critical temperature specifically, 4 Kelvin (about −269◦C). The only substance
able to easily reach this temperature is liquid helium.
Physical Property: Helium Expansion
Helium behaves very differently as a liquid compared to its gaseous state.
• Liquid Helium: Maintains the temperature of 4K.
• Gaseous Helium: Immediately warms up to room temperature.
The critical safety factor is the expansion ratio: one liter of liquid helium boils to
700 liters of gas at room temperature. This rapid expansion can create extremely high
pressure inside the magnet.
Insulation Evolution (The Thermos Concept)
If liquid helium were placed in an ordinary container, it would boil away within minutes. To
preserve it, advanced insulation technologies are used:
1. Vacuum: The helium is held in an internal vessel surrounded by an external vessel,
with the air evacuated between them (vacuum insulation) to prevent heat transfer by
conduction. This can extend the helium’s lifetime to about a month, but that’s still not
economical.
53

content:
Chapter 6. Advanced Magnet Operations: Cooling, Ramping, and Safety
54
2. Cold Head: This is a mechanical cooling system that works to reduce boil-off to an
absolute minimum.
6.1.2
Cold Head Technology
The Cold Head acts like a specialized refrigerator. It uses a helium gas compressor to circulate
pressurized helium gas and cool various thermal shields surrounding the helium vessel.
Old vs. New Technology
• Standard Cold Head (Old): This system cools only the thermal shields (to about 20K
and 80K). It reduces, but does not prevent, helium boil-off. The magnet requires periodic
refilling every 3-4 months to replace lost helium.
• Zero Boil-off Technology (New/Reliquefying): In modern systems, evaporated he-
lium gas is routed to a very cold region (4K) inside the cold head.
– When the helium gas contacts this cold area, it recondenses back into a liquid.
– The condensed liquid drips back into the tank.
– The result: virtually no helium loss (zero boil-off) as long as the system operates
properly.
Pressure Control Mechanism
If the recondensation is too eﬀicient, all the helium gas could become liquid, creating
negative pressure inside the vessel. This is dangerous, as it can draw in outside air which
could freeze and block vents. To prevent this, a fine electronic heater is installed. If the
pressure drops below a safe limit, the heater evaporates a small amount of helium to raise
the pressure and keep it stable (positive pressure).
6.1.3
Magnet Ramping (Energizing the Superconducting Coil)
After cooling the magnet, the electrical current (e.g., 500 Amperes) needs to be injected so that
it circulates indefinitely within the superconducting coil. This process is called Ramping.
The Superconducting Switch
Inside the magnet, there is a special superconducting switch (a piece of superconductive material
connected in parallel with the coil).
1. Connect Power Supply: Connect the external power supply.
2. Heat the Switch: Heat up this small switch, causing it to transition from a supercon-
ductor to a resistive material.
3. Injection: The current from the power source now has two paths: through the coil (zero
resistance) and through the switch (high resistance). Naturally, most current will flow
through the easier (coil) path.
4. Ramp Up: Gradually increase the current until reaching the required value (Target
Field).
