content:
Chapter 6. Advanced Magnet Operations: Cooling, Ramping, and Safety
55
5. Cool the Switch: Stop heating the switch so it turns back into a superconductor (zero
resistance).
6. Disconnect: Now the current circulates in a closed loop within the magnet and the
switch, without any loss. You can safely disconnect the power supply, and the magnetic
field will persist (Persistent Mode).
Maintenance Alert: The Helium Adsorber
The helium compressor does not just move gas; it uses oil for cooling and lubrication.
The Adsorber is a high-grade filter designed to trap oil vapor.
• The Risk: If the adsorber is not replaced (typically every 18,000 hours), oil vapor
will reach the Cold Head. At 4K, this oil freezes instantly, blocking the cooling
cycle.
• The Result: The magnet will lose cooling, pressure will spike, and a spontaneous
quench will occur.
• Pro-Tip: Always check the adsorber pressure and date during every preventive
maintenance (PM) visit.
6.1.4
Cooling a ”Warm” Magnet
If the magnet warms up and reaches room temperature (for example, after a quench or extended
outage), how do we cool it down? It is not possible to pour in liquid helium directly. The hot
metal would cause it to boil off instantly, making it prohibitively expensive.
Proper pre-cooling steps:
1. Liquid Nitrogen Phase”Obsolete”: First, fill the magnet with liquid nitrogen.
• It is inexpensive.
• Its temperature is 77 K
(−196◦C).
• It
cools
the
magnet
from 300 K to 77 K.
2. Purging: Completely drain the nitrogen and thoroughly clean the vessel.
3. Liquid Helium Phase: Now fill with liquid helium, cooling from 77K down to 4K. This
stage is called ”bottom fill,” using a special siphon introduced from below to ensure gradual
and eﬀicient cooling.
Low-Inventory (Dry) Magnets
The traditional ”liquid bath” magnet (using 1,500+ liters of helium) is being replaced by
Low-Inventory or Dry Magnet technology (e.g., Philips BlueSeal or GE Freelium).
• The 7-Liter Revolution: These magnets use a micro-cooling circuit containing
only 7 to 20 liters of helium, which is sealed for life at the factory.
• Advantage: Because there is so little helium, they do not require a Quench Pipe
(vent) to the roof, making them much easier and cheaper to install in high-rise
buildings.
• Maintenance: They never require ”refilling” or cryogen monitoring, significantly
reducing long-term operational costs.

Chapter 7
Medical Informatics: PACS,
DICOM, and the Digital Workflow
7.1
The Transition to the Digital Era
The evolution of medical imaging from analog film to digital datasets represents a fundamental
paradigm shift in patient care. Historically, MRI acquisition was a bottlenecked, ”film-based”
process relying on chemical development and the physical logistics of warehouse archival. To-
day, the MRI scanner serves as the initiating sensor for a complex, high-throughput digital
information chain.
The Paradigm Shift: Film vs. PACS
The transition to a dynamic PACS-based workflow unlocks transformative advantages:
1. Instant Access and Sharing: Simultaneous local and remote (teleradiology) ac-
cess to the same dataset without delay.
2. Advanced Post-Processing: Digital images support windowing, 3D reconstruc-
tion, and quantitative analysis beyond film limitations.
3. Data Security and Durability: RAID-based digital archives ensure high avail-
ability and protect against physical degradation and data loss.

7.2
The Integrated Hospital Information Ecosystem
A modern MRI system functions as a critical, high-volume node within a cohesive hospital-
wide digital architecture. For a complete diagnostic cycle to occur, four specialized information
systems must achieve seamless, automated interoperability.
• HIS (Hospital Information System): This is the enterprise-level administrative sys-
tem of record. It governs global patient registration, cross-departmental scheduling, and
financial/billing operations.
• RIS (Radiology Information System): The department-specific workflow engine. It
interfaces directly with the modality to push the Modality Worklist (MWL) to the MRI
machine, eliminating manual data entry errors. Crucially, it also houses the final, signed
textual radiology report.
• PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication System): The dedicated infrastruc-
ture responsible for the high-speed ingress, secure long-term storage, eﬀicient retrieval, and
distribution of image data.
• EHR (Electronic Health Record) vs. EMR (Electronic Medical Record): The
EMR is typically a siloed, digital chart confined to a single practice. The EHR is designed
for advanced interoperability, creating a longitudinal, comprehensive patient history shared
securely across multiple unaﬀiliated providers and facilities.

Chapter 7. Medical Informatics: PACS, DICOM, and the Digital Workflow
59
7.3
DICOM: The Universal Technical Foundation
The prerequisite for cross-vendor interoperability—allowing an MRI from Vendor X to com-
municate flawlessly with a PACS from Vendor Y—is strict adherence to the DICOM (Digital
Imaging and Communications in Medicine) standard.
7.3.1
SOP Classes, IODs, and Services
DICOM communication is formally structured around the SOP (Service-Object Pair) Class,
which binds a command to a specific data type.
• IOD (Information Object Definition): This defines the data Object—the structure
of the image pixels and the mandatory metadata tags in the header (e.g., Patient Name,
Acquisition Date).
• DIMSE (DICOM Service Elements): These are the low-level Services or commands
that facilitate the exchange (e.g., C-STORE for image upload, C-FIND for database
query).
• SOP Class: The formal pairing, such as the MR Image Storage SOP Class. A failure
in the handshake is often due to a mismatch in the specific version of the SOP Class
supported by both parties.
7.3.2
Metadata Integrity: The Role of Unique Identifiers (UIDs)
Every discrete entity within the DICOM structure is assigned a globally unique, vendor-neutral
numerical string: the UID. This numbering scheme prevents critical data collision.
• Structure and Collision Risk: UIDs contain an organization root (identifying the
source facility/vendor) and a suﬀix (identifying the specific instance). If a PACS receives
two distinct image sets that erroneously share the same Study Instance UID, the system
will typically reject the second submission or, more dangerously, silently overwrite the
first, leading to gaps in the patient’s historical archive.

7.4
PACS Deployment Architectures
The physical deployment of a PACS is tailored to the organization’s scale, latency tolerance,
and regulatory environment.
1. Client-Server Model (Centralized): The dominant architecture. Images are consoli-
dated onto a central, high-availability server cluster. Workstations operate as ”thin clients”
or ”fat clients,” initiating a Query/Retrieve (C-FIND/C-MOVE) request to pull the data
only upon a radiologist’s explicit action.
2. Distributed System (Peer-to-Peer): Images are pushed directly from the modality
to pre-configured, designated reading stations. While this minimizes server load and op-
timizes local reading speed, it mandates rigorous background synchronization services to
ensure the local station’s data is correctly reflected in the central repository, mitigating
data fragmentation risk.
3. Web/Cloud-Based Systems (Modern Scalability): Leveraging standard HTTP(S)
protocols (DICOMweb), storage and the viewing application are hosted externally. This
architecture excels in Scalability and facilitates seamless Teleradiology access, though it
introduces new reliance on Internet Service Provider (ISP) bandwidth and stringent cloud
security posture.

• Hanging Protocols: A highly customized software configuration that acts as the radiolo-

monitors for comparison (e.g., aligning the current T2-weighted sequence with the T2 from
a prior study).

• Image Manipulation Suite: Foundational tools include Window/Level adjustment (ma-
nipulating the pixel value mapping to display contrast), Zoom/Pan, and geometric/area
measurements.
• Advanced Post-Processing Techniques: These tools move imaging beyond 2D slicing:
– MPR (Multiplanar Reconstruction): Mathematically generating orthogonal (Coro-
nal, Sagittal) or oblique cross-sections from the initial axial volumetric acquisition
data.
– MIP (Maximum Intensity Projection): A technique that renders the highest
signal intensity voxel along any projection line, effectively ”seeing through” lower-
density tissue to highlight contrast-filled structures, standard in MR Angiography
(MRA).
– Volume Rendering (VR): Sophisticated algorithms that generate semi-photorealistic
3D surface models, crucial for complex surgical planning and spatial anatomical cor-
relation.
Figure 7.5: Demonstration of Advanced Visualization: Multiplanar Reconstruction (MPR),
Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), and 3D Volume Rendering.
7.6
The IT Infrastructure Backbone
Managing the sheer volume of high-resolution MRI data (often > 100MB per study) demands
a robust physical and logical infrastructure.
• Storage and Redundancy (RAID): Storage arrays utilize RAID configurations to en-
sure data redundancy. Standard practice incorporates Tiered Storage, placing the most fre-
quently accessed, recent studies on high-speed SSD/SAS arrays, while older, less-accessed
studies are migrated to slower, high-capacity (SATA) archival tiers.
• Network Throughput: To prevent I/O bottlenecks during peak data transfers, the
infrastructure relies on high-speed switching fabric, typically 10Gbps Ethernet backbone
connections, often utilizing Fiber Optic cabling for long-distance, high-integrity data trans-
mission.
• Diagnostic Display Integrity: Radiologist workstations must utilize medical-grade,
high-luminance monitors (≥3MP). These displays require periodic, automated calibration
using a photometer to strictly maintain the DICOM Part 14 Grayscale Standard Display
Function, ensuring contrast representation is consistent and diagnostically reliable across
all viewing platforms.

7.7
Operational Integrity: Troubleshooting and Maintenance
Workflow disruption most commonly occurs at the junction between the imaging device and the
archive, centering on network configuration or DICOM protocol adherence.
7.7.1
Connectivity and DICOM Handshake Verification
When image transfer fails, an engineer executes a tiered validation process to isolate the fault
domain:
1. Verify the ”Holy Trinity” (Static Configuration): The three critical parameters
shared between the MRI and PACS must match exactly:
• AE Title: Unique Application Entity Title (Case-Sensitive).
• IP Address: Static network address.
• Port Number: The listening communication port.
2. Physical Layer Test (Ping): Confirm baseline TCP/IP connectivity.
3. Application Layer Test (C-ECHO): If the Ping is successful but the C-ECHO (DI-
COM Ping) fails, the Port is likely blocked by a firewall or the PACS application is not
actively listening.
4. Transfer Layer Validation (C-STORE): If the handshake succeeds but the image
transfer fails, check for storage capacity exhaustion or Transfer Syntax incompatibility (an
agreement failure on compression encoding).
The Static IP Mandate
Modality and PACS server IP addresses must never be assigned via DHCP. A dynamic IP
change automatically invalidates the configuration on the receiving PACS, which enforces
a security block against the now ”unknown” IP, leading to immediate, complete failure
of image transmission.

content:
Chapter 7. Medical Informatics: PACS, DICOM, and the Digital Workflow
63
7.7.2
Modern Cloud Integration: DICOMweb Troubleshooting
For cloud-hosted PACS, troubleshooting migrates from port/IP management to Web service
authentication and URL validation:
• QIDO-RS (Query): Failures often stem from an incorrect service Endpoint URL or a
revoked/expired TLS/SSL security certificate required for secure HTTPS communication.
• STOW-RS (Store): Requires validating the service account’s allocated Write Permis-
sions within the cloud environment, or debugging malformed metadata violating the
RESTful STOW-RS structure.
7.8
Data Governance: Privacy, Security, and Anonymization
Protecting the integrity and confidentiality of patient data is a continuous compliance mandate
(e.g., HIPAA, GDPR).
• Security Posture: Requires proactive implementation of Role-Based Access Control
(RBAC), ensuring least-privilege access, supplemented by rigorous security audits to log
all access attempts. High-privilege accounts require Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA).
• De-identification for Research: When exporting images for teaching or research, a
process called Anonymization must occur. This involves aggressive Metadata Cleaning
of header tags (Name, ID, DOB). A significant challenge is Pixel Data Scrubbing—the
physical blurring or blacking out of patient identifiers that vendors sometimes burn directly
into the image pixels.
• Data Retention Strategy: Despite removing direct identifiers, engineers often must
strategically Retain UIDs or Longitudinal Temporal Info to preserve the ability to compare
a series of scans over time for research cohorts, without compromising the patient’s identity.
The Value Proposition of Digital Integration
The complete digital integration of the MRI workflow yields systemic improvements:
1. Operational Eﬀiciency: Automated MWL reduces manual labor and adminis-
trative reporting errors.
2. Diagnostic Augmentation: Advanced 3D post-processing allows for novel spatial
correlations previously impossible.
3. Global Reach: Secure, high-fidelity image transfer enables expert consultation
regardless of the patient’s physical location.
Fundamentals of MRI

content:
Chapter 8
Safety and Emergency Procedures
Safety in the MRI environment is unique due to the ”always-on” nature of the superconducting
magnet. Unlike X-ray or CT systems, the primary hazard ”the static magnetic field” is invisible,
persistent, and cannot be turned off by a standard power switch.
This chapter details the
dynamics of magnet quenches, engineering protocols for ramping, and critical patient screening
procedures.
8.1
Magnet Quench Dynamics
A Quench is the sudden and rapid loss of superconductivity in the magnet coil. In a supercon-
ducting state, current flows with zero resistance. However, if any portion of the coil transitions
to a resistive state (becoming ”normal”), the massive kinetic energy of the circulating electrons
is converted into heat.
8.1.1
Mechanism of a Quench
The transition from superconductivity to resistance follows a catastrophic feedback loop:
1. Initial Trigger: Localized heating occurs, often due to a microscopic shift in the coil
windings (”flux jumping”) or a failure in the cryogenic cooling system.
2. Phase Transition: As the temperature rises above the critical threshold (approximately
9 K for Niobium-Titanium), the wire gains electrical resistance.
3. Ohmic Heating: The high current (typically 500+ Amperes) passing through this resis-
tive point produces enormous heat via H = I2R losses.
4. Boil-off: This heat is rapidly transferred to the surrounding liquid helium, causing it to
boil and transition into a gaseous state instantly.
5. Gas Expansion: Helium gas expands at a ratio of 1:700 compared to its liquid form.
This creates extreme internal pressure within the cryostat.
8.1.2
Safety Infrastructure: Venting and Valves
To prevent the cryostat from exploding due to extreme internal pressure, MRI systems are
equipped with specialized pressure-relief hardware:
• Burst Disk (Quench Valve): A calibrated carbon or metal disk designed to rupture at
a specific pressure, providing an immediate exit path for the expanding gas.
64

metadata.manual: Copy of Mribookv1.3.pdf

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p65_c71
content:
Chapter 8. Safety and Emergency Procedures
65
• Quench Pipe: A large-diameter, vacuum-insulated exhaust duct that directs the ex-
tremely cold helium gas (−269◦C) from the magnet to a safe location outside the building.
Asphyxiation and Pressure Hazard
If a Quench Pipe fails or leaks into the scan room, the expanding helium will rapidly
displace oxygen. This creates a risk of asphyxiation. Furthermore, the sudden pressure
increase in the room can make it physically impossible to open the door (which usually
opens inward) until a window is broken or a pressure-relief vent activates.
8.2
Emergency Shutdown Protocols
MRI facilities distinguish between two types of emergency stops: the Emergency Electrical
Stop (which cuts power to the electronics but leaves the magnetic field active) and the Magnet
Stop.
8.2.1
The Emergency Run-Down Unit (ERDU)
The ”Quench Button,” or ERDU, is reserved for life-threatening emergencies where a person is
pinned against the magnet by a ferromagnetic object (e.g., an oxygen tank, a gurney, or a floor
buffer).
Pressing this button activates internal heaters within the cryostat to force a controlled
quench, ”dumping” the magnetic field within seconds. Note: Triggering a quench is an ex-
pensive event, often costing upwards of $50,000 to $100,000 in helium loss, engineering labor,
and equipment downtime.
8.2.2
Magnetic Field Ramping Safety
The process of energizing the magnet (Ramping) is a high-risk operation performed by service
engineers. It involves the use of physical High-Current Leads to connect an external power
supply to the internal superconducting coils.
Key Engineering Hazards:
• Electrical Arcing: If the leads are dirty or poorly seated, the 500A current can create a
massive electrical arc. The resulting heat can trigger an unplanned quench.
• Persistent Mode Verification: An engineer must never remove the current leads until
the superconducting switch has been cooled and the system is verified to be in Persistent
Mode (current circulating in a closed loop).
• Disconnection Protocol: The power supply current must be ramped to zero and the
magnet field stability confirmed before the physical leads are disconnected.
8.3
Patient Screening and Bio-effects
The primary safety role of the technologist is to screen for ”hidden” hazards that can cause
thermal injury or permanent internal damage when exposed to the magnetic and radiofrequency
(RF) fields.
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p66_c72
content:
Chapter 8. Safety and Emergency Procedures
66
8.3.1
Conductive Materials and Thermal Injury
The oscillating RF field (B1) can induce electrical currents in conductive materials, leading to
RF heating and skin burns.
• Tattoos and Makeup: Older tattoos and certain cosmetics (especially eyeliner) may
contain iron oxide or metallic flakes. These can heat up during the scan. Patients are
advised to use cold compresses or, in some cases, defer the scan.
• Transdermal Patches: Many medication patches (e.g., nicotine, hormone, or pain relief)
contain a thin aluminum foil backing to control drug release. The RF field can heat this
foil, causing significant second-degree burns. All such patches must be removed before
the patient enters the bore.
8.3.2
Special Considerations
• Pregnancy: While there is no evidence of ionizing radiation or teratogenic effects from
MRI, it is standard practice to avoid scanning during the first trimester (the period of
organogenesis) as a precaution, unless the clinical benefit clearly outweighs the theoretical
risk.
• Implants: Any implantable device (pacemakers, cochlear implants, neurostimulators)
must be verified as MR Conditional at the specific field strength (1.5T vs 3.0T) and
checked for specific SAR (Specific Absorption Rate) limits before the scan proceeds.
Fundamentals of MRI

content:
Chapter 9
MRI Artifacts
9.1
Introduction to Artifacts
In Magnetic Resonance Imaging, an artifact is any feature in an image that does not correspond
to the spatial distribution of tissue in the imaged plane. Recognizing these artifacts is crucial
not only for diagnosis but for distinguishing between incorrect patient positioning, parameter
selection errors, and system hardware failures.
Artifacts can be broadly categorized into three sources:
1. Patient-related: Motion, flow.
2. Signal Processing-related: Aliasing, chemical shift, truncation.
3. Hardware-related: RF interference, magnetic field inhomogeneity.
9.2
Patient and Physiological Artifacts
9.2.1
Motion Artifact
Figure 9.1: Motion artifact causing blurring and ghosting along the phase-encode axis.
Patient movement (voluntary or involuntary, such as respiration or cardiac pulsation) during
the acquisition process is the most common cause of poor image quality.
• Appearance: Blurring or ”ghosting” (replicas of anatomy) propagating specifically in
the Phase-Encoding direction. This occurs because the time between phase-encoding
steps (TR) is long, allowing motion to occur, whereas frequency encoding is instantaneous.
67

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p68_c74
content:
Chapter 9. MRI Artifacts
68
• Solution:
– Patient education and immobilization pads.
– Use of Saturation Bands (Sat Bands) over moving areas (e.g., chest).
– Respiratory Gating or Breath-hold sequences.
– Swap phase/frequency directions to move the artifact away from the region of interest.
9.2.2
Magnetic Susceptibility Artifacts
Figure 9.2: Example of susceptibility artifact due to metal, showing signal void and distortion.
Magnetic susceptibility refers to the ability of a substance to become magnetized. Artifacts
arise when adjacent tissues have vastly different susceptibilities (e.g., air/tissue or metal/tissue),
causing local distortions in the B0 field.
• Appearance: Large signal voids (black holes) and bright pile-up of signal, often accom-
panied by severe geometric distortion.
• Common Causes: Dental fillings, surgical clips, orthopedic implants, or the interface
between the sinuses and the brain.
• Solution:
– Remove removable metal objects.
– Use Spin Echo (SE) sequences instead of Gradient Echo (GRE), as the 180◦pulse
rephases spins dephased by inhomogeneity.
– Use lower TE (Echo Time).
– Use specialized Metal Artifact Reduction Sequences (MARS).
9.3
Signal Processing and Sampling Artifacts
9.3.1
Aliasing (Wrap-Around)
Aliasing occurs when the Field of View (FOV) is smaller than the anatomy being imaged. Tissue
outside the FOV is still excited but is undersampled.
Fundamentals of MRI

content:
Chapter 9. MRI Artifacts
69
• Appearance: Anatomy that exists outside the FOV ”wraps around” to the opposite side
of the image (e.g., the patient’s nose appears in the back of their head).
• Physics: Frequencies outside the Nyquist limit are interpreted as lower frequencies on
the opposite side of the spectrum.
• Solution:
– Increase the FOV.
– Use ”No Phase Wrap” or Oversampling options (this samples a larger area in
the phase direction and discards the edges).
Figure 9.3: Aliasing artifact where the arm wraps around into the abdomen.
9.3.2
Chemical Shift Artifact
Figure 9.4: Showing characteristic dark and bright bands at fat-muscle interfaces.
Fat and water protons precess at slightly different frequencies ( 3.5 ppm difference).
In
the frequency-encoding direction, the scanner maps spatial position based on frequency. The
scanner mistakenly maps fat protons to a position slightly shifted from water protons.
• Appearance: A dark band on one side of a structure (e.g., kidney or muscle) and a bright
band on the opposite side.
• Solution:

content:
Chapter 9. MRI Artifacts
70
– Increase the Receiver Bandwidth (reduces the pixel shift).
– Use Fat Saturation (FatSat) techniques to null the fat signal.
9.3.3
Partial Volume Effect
Figure 9.5: Blurring the optic nerve (left) compared to a sharper image using thinner slices
(right).
The partial volume effect occurs when multiple tissues with differing signal intensities are
present within a single voxel.
• Appearance: The resulting signal represents an average of these tissues, leading to a
blurring of boundaries and reduced contrast.
• Solution: Use thinner slices or higher matrix sizes (reducing voxel volume).
9.3.4
Gibbs Ringing (Truncation Artifact)
Figure 9.6: (pseudo-syrinx) mimicking pathology (left), corrected by increasing the matrix size
(right).
This occurs at high-contrast interfaces (e.g., Spinal cord vs. CSF, or Skull vs. Brain) due to
undersampling of high spatial frequencies (finite number of encoding steps).
• Appearance: Parallel lines or ”ripples” adjacent to a high-contrast edge. It can mimic a
syrinx in the spinal cord.
• Solution: Increase the matrix size (scan with higher resolution) or use raw data filters.
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p71_c77
content:
Chapter 9. MRI Artifacts
71
9.4
Hardware and Room Artifacts
9.4.1
Zipper Artifact (RF Interference)
Figure 9.7: Zipper artifact appearing as a band of noise, caused by external RF interference.
This is a critical artifact for maintenance engineers as it indicates a failure in system shielding.
Maintenance Alert: The Zipper
The Zipper artifact is caused by external Radio Frequency (RF) waves leaking into the
scan room and interfering with the signal.
• Appearance: A dense line of alternating noise (looking like a zipper) extending across
the image in the phase-encoding direction.
• Causes:
– The magnet room door is not fully closed or the RF seal is damaged.
– An electronic device (patient monitor, pulse ox) inside the room is emitting RF.
– A burnt-out lightbulb in the scan room (flickering filament).
– Breach in the Faraday cage.
• Solution: Close the door properly. Remove unauthorized electronics. If persistent, call
an RF shielding engineer.
9.4.2
Cross-Talk (Slice Overlap)
When acquiring multiple slices, the RF pulses are not perfectly rectangular. If slices are placed
too close together, the excitation pulse of one slice may partially excite the protons in the
adjacent slice.
• Appearance: Reduced signal intensity (darkness) in specific slices within a stack.
• Solution: Introduce a ”slice gap” (usually 10% to 20% of slice thickness) or use interleaved
acquisition (acquiring slices 1, 3, 5 then 2, 4, 6).
Fundamentals of MRI

content:
Example: The Sagittal Locator Check
Perform a single-slice sagittal spin echo of the phantom. What to look for:
• On the image, you should see crossed 45-degree wedges.
• Pass Criteria: Both wedges should appear with equal intensity.
• Fail Criteria: If one wedge is darker or faded, or the phantom appears tilted, the
phantom must be re-centered, re-leveled, and re-scanned.
This confirms that the slice location is exactly at the magnet’s isocenter.

• A sphere filled with liquid, used to test spatial uniformity of radiofrequency (RF)
transmission and reception fields. The transmit field (RF B1T) is the B1 field used
to rotate the magnetization, and the receive field (RF B1R) reflects the sensitivity

When scanning the standard ACR (American College of Radiology) Phantom, the technolo-
gist must look for specific geometric markers to ensure the gradients are linear and the table
positioning is accurate.
Example: The Sagittal Locator Check
Perform a single-slice sagittal spin echo of the phantom. What to look for:
• On the image, you should see crossed 45-degree wedges.
• Pass Criteria: Both wedges should appear with equal intensity.
• Fail Criteria: If one wedge is darker or faded, or the phantom appears tilted, the
phantom must be re-centered, re-leveled, and re-scanned.
This confirms that the slice location is exactly at the magnet’s isocenter.

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p75_t83
content:
Example: Geometric Accuracy Check (The Grid Test)
Perform an axial T1-weighted scan of the phantom (usually focusing on Slice 5).
What to look for:
• A square Grid/Lattice pattern across the field of view.
• Pass Criteria: All horizontal and vertical lines must be perfectly straight. The
measured diameter of the phantom grid should be within ±2mm of its actual size
(190mm).
• Fail Criteria: If the lines on the grid look like they are ”bowing,” ”bending,”
or ”warped,” the system has failed geometric accuracy.
Root Cause: This indicates that the Gradients are out of calibration (Gradient
Non-linearity). This is a far more common failure in clinical practice than the wedges
having unequal intensity.

10.2.1
Cleaning Protocols
• Do not use strong alcohol or harsh chemicals on plastic surfaces or coils. Use only mild
cleaning solutions and a damp cloth.
• Clean the filters for cooling fans regularly to prevent overheating.
• Wipe the patient table and all surfaces that come into contact with patients after every
scan.

To ensure the machine functions eﬀiciently, a strict and periodic maintenance schedule must
be followed (as specified in the manufacturer’s protocols). The following is a suggested routine

Common Faults and Troubleshooting

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p76_c86
content:
Chapter 10. Calibration and Maintenance Protocols
76
10.3.1
Mechanical Malfunctions
The most important mechanical malfunctions that may occur include:
1. Hydraulic Table Faults: Problems with the hydraulic oil pump that raises/lowers the
table, faulty seals, or failure of the table to move in the required directions.
2. Microswitch and Limit Switch Failures: Damage to the precision switches or end-of-
travel (limit) switches found in the table, which are used to define travel limits.
3. Cooling System Faults:
• Fault in the helium cold head unit, requiring its replacement and leading to system
shutdown, pressure increase in the magnet, and helium loss.
• Fault in the water chiller unit, which requires regular maintenance and cleaning of
filters if overheating is observed.
• Presence of contaminants in the helium unit filters, revealed by increased tempera-
tures and requiring regular cleaning of the filters.
4. Laser Printer Malfunctions: Mechanical faults in the printer requiring calibration or
servicing.
5. Film Developer Malfunction: Faults can arise from accumulated dirt or debris, requir-
ing cleaning and maintenance.
10.3.2
Electrical Malfunctions
The main possible electrical faults include:
1. RF Unit/Amplifier Failure: Problems with the RF generator, vacuum tube, or RF
amplifier. This can cause blown fuses, dark images, or high noise due to weak excitation
signals.
2. Gradient Unit/Amplifier Failure: Usually appears as the complete absence of images,
or images may only appear in some directions but not others. It can also lead to image
distortions (geometric distortion). The system may halt automatically if this occurs.
3. Image Artifacts: Appearance of unwanted lines or noise in images, commonly caused
by grounding issues or leakage of external RF signals (RF shielding breach).
Temperature & Power
Electrical failures are rare due to the Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS). However, any
mechanical failure in the cooling system can cause overheating, which automatically
stops the device electrically for protection.
10.4
Troubleshooting Mobile Unit Environmental Controls
The following tables address issues related to the mobile unit’s internal environment, specifically
humidity and Temperature. The humidity settings for the mobile unit are 30% RH to 60% RH.
The desired room temperature is 22.2°C.

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p79_c91
content:
Chapter 11
Advanced Imaging Techniques
11.1
Introduction: Beyond Anatomy
Until now, we have primarily discussed Anatomical (Structural) MRI. These techniques (T1-
weighted, T2-weighted) provide information to qualitatively and quantitatively describe the
shape, size, and integrity of gray and white matter structures.
Figure 11.1: Structural MRI allows for clear differentiation between Gray Matter (GM), White
Matter (WM), and Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF).
However, modern MRI is capable of much more than just static anatomy. It can visualize
the function of organs, the microscopic movement of water, and the flow of blood.
11.2
Functional MRI (fMRI)
Functional MRI (fMRI) measures brain activity by detecting changes associated with blood flow.
11.2.1
Basic Principle: BOLD Contrast
The primary contrast mechanism used in fMRI is BOLD (Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent).
79

metadata.device: Copy Of Mribookv1.3
metadata.manual: Copy of Mribookv1.3.pdf

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p80_c92
content:
Chapter 11. Advanced Imaging Techniques
80
Figure 11.2: Example of a functional MRI scan showing brain activity superimposed on anatomy.
Physiological Basis: Hemodynamic Response
1. When a region of the brain is active (e.g., thinking, moving, seeing), blood flow to
this area increases.
2. Oxygen consumption increases, but the blood supply increases even more. This
leads to a local increase in oxygenated blood relative to deoxygenated blood.
3. Deoxygenated hemoglobin is paramagnetic. It disturbs the local magnetic field
homogeneity, causing a quicker loss of signal (shorter T ∗
2 ).
4. Oxygenated hemoglobin is diamagnetic and has magnetic properties similar to
tissue. Therefore, active areas with more oxygenated blood produce a higher MR
signal compared to inactive areas.
11.2.2
Stimulus and Response
fMRI is typically used for research or pre-surgical planning. Data is acquired by alternating
between ”rest” and ”activation” states (e.g., tapping a finger, looking at a flashing light). The
signal changes are very small (1–5%) but can be detected statistically to identify active brain
regions.
Figure 11.3: Hemodynamic response function: Signal changes in response to stimuli over time.
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p81_c93
content:
Chapter 11. Advanced Imaging Techniques
81
11.2.3
Practical fMRI Considerations
1.
Resting State Instructions Unlike task-based fMRI (where the patient taps a finger),
”Resting State” fMRI looks at the brain’s background connectivity.
• The Instruction: ”Keep your eyes open and focus on a crosshair or point on the mirror.
Do not fall asleep.”
• Why? Closing eyes increases the risk of sleep (which changes brain activity) and can
induce alpha-wave oscillations that disturb the resting state signal.
2.
Distortion Correction (Reverse Phase Encoding) Echo Planar Imaging (EPI)
sequences used for fMRI are very fast but prone to geometric distortion (stretching/squishing
of the brain image), especially near air-filled sinuses.
The ”Blip-Up / Blip-Down” Technique
To correct this, technicians often acquire two B0 field maps or two fMRI reference scans
with opposite Phase Encoding directions:
• Scan 1: Phase Encoding Right ≫Left (Distortion stretches one way).
• Scan 2: Phase Encoding Left ≫Right (Distortion stretches the opposite way).
During image processing, the computer combines these two images to calculate a ”distor-
tion map” and mathematically un-stretch the image to its true anatomical shape.
11.3
Diffusion Weighted Imaging (DWI)
Diffusion Weighted Imaging (DWI) is an extremely sensitive technique that detects the micro-
scopic random motion of water molecules (Brownian motion) within tissues.
Figure 11.4: Visualizing water diffusion: Isotropic (free) vs. Anisotropic (restricted).
11.3.1
Isotropic vs. Anisotropic Diffusion
• Isotropic diffusion: Water molecules move freely in all directions. This is seen in fluids
such as the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the brain’s ventricles.
• Anisotropic diffusion: Water molecule movement is restricted or preferentially directed
along a specific axis. For example, in the white matter, cell membranes and myelin sheaths
restrict water to move primarily along the length of the nerve axons.
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p82_c94
content:
Chapter 11. Advanced Imaging Techniques
82
11.3.2
Physics of Diffusion Gradients
To detect this motion, several diffusion gradients are applied (often along 3 to 60+ directions).
• For each direction, we use two strong, opposite gradient pulses.
• Stationary molecules: The phase shift caused by the first gradient is perfectly cancelled
by the second. Signal is preserved.
• Moving molecules: Because they move to a new location between the two pulses, the
gradients do not cancel out. Phase coherence is lost, and the signal is attenuated.
The signal attenuation is described by the equation:
Sb
S0
= exp(−b · ADC)
(11.1)
Where b is a factor related to the strength/duration of the gradients (the ”b-value”), and ADC
is the Apparent Diffusion Coeﬀicient.
11.3.3
Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI)
By measuring diffusion in many directions, we can reconstruct the tracts of white matter fibers
in 3D. This is called Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI).
(a) Diffusion gradients principle
(b) Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI)
Figure 11.5: Diffusion MRI: gradient encoding and tensor-based tract visualization
11.3.4
Clinical Application: Stroke
DWI is the gold standard for the early diagnosis of ischemic (acute) stroke.
Stroke Diagnosis
In a stroke, the sodium-potassium pumps in cells fail, causing water to rush into the cells.
This swelling (cytotoxic edema) restricts the movement of water molecules. Because the
water cannot move, the diffusion gradients do not attenuate the signal. Result: The stroke
area appears bright (hyperintense) on DWI images within minutes of onset, whereas
CT might appear normal for hours.
Fundamentals of MRI

content:
Chapter 11. Advanced Imaging Techniques
83
11.4
MR Angiography (MRA)
(a) MRA of neck vasculature
(b) MRA of legs
MR Angiography (MRA) is a technique for visualizing blood vessels (arteries and veins) with
high clarity.
• Contrast-Enhanced MRA: Uses a gadolinium-based contrast agent to shorten T1 re-
laxation time of blood, making vessels appear very bright on T1-weighted scans.
• Non-Contrast MRA: Relies on the flow of fresh, unsaturated spins flowing into the
imaging slice to generate high signal compared to stationary background tissue.
11.5
Cardiac MRI
Figure 11.7: Cardiac MRI.
Cardiac MRI provides a non-invasive assessment of the function and structure of the car-
diovascular system.
It is complex because the heart is moving (beating) and the patient is
breathing. It requires:
• ECG Gating: To synchronize imaging with the heartbeat (freezing motion).
• Respiratory Gating/Breath-holds: To minimize chest motion.
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p84_c96
content:
Chapter 11. Advanced Imaging Techniques
84
11.6
Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS)
While standard MRI creates images of the anatomy (water and fat distribution), Magnetic
Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) is a technique that provides information about the chemical
composition of the tissue.
Metabolic ”Biopsy”
MRS is often called a ”virtual biopsy.” Instead of producing an image of the brain’s shape,
it produces a spectrum (a graph) that represents the concentration of specific metabolites
(chemicals) in a selected voxel.
11.6.1
Clinical Utility
MRS is primarily used in brain imaging to evaluate:
• Tumors: Differentiating between tumor recurrence and radiation necrosis.
• Metabolic Disorders: Diagnosing conditions like hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
• Epilepsy: Localizing seizure focus.
11.6.2
Key Metabolites
The spectrum displays peaks corresponding to different chemicals. The most common markers
include:
• NAA (N-acetyl aspartate): A marker of neuronal health.
Reduced levels indicate
neuronal loss (e.g., Alzheimer’s, stroke).
• Choline (Cho): A marker of cell membrane turnover.
Elevated levels often indicate
rapid cell division (tumors).
• Creatine (Cr): Used as a reference control because its levels remain relatively stable.
• Lactate (Lac): Indicates anaerobic metabolism; usually seen in ischemia (stroke) or
aggressive tumors.
11.7
Neuromelanin-Sensitive MRI (NM-MRI)
While standard T1 and T2 sequences provide excellent structural data, they often fail to visualize
specific substructures of the midbrain, such as the Substantia Nigra (SN). This is critical for
diagnosing neurodegenerative disorders like Parkinson’s Disease.
What is Neuromelanin?
Neuromelanin is a dark pigment found in specific neurons (dopaminergic neurons) of the
substantia nigra.
It has paramagnetic properties (T1-shortening effects).
By using a
specific pulse sequence, we can make the substantia nigra appear bright (hyperintense)
against the background tissue. Loss of this brightness indicates a loss of neurons (Parkin-
son’s).
Fundamentals of MRI

Creatine, Choline).
11.7.1
Acquisition Technique
To visualize Neuromelanin, a 2D T2* Gradient Recalled Echo (GRE) sequence is used combined
with a Magnetization Transfer (MT) preparation pulse.
Critical Slice Positioning: Scanning the entire brain is unnecessary and time-consuming.
Coverage is limited to the midbrain.
1. Locate the sagittal plane showing the largest gap between the Thalamus and the Midbrain.
2. Align slices parallel to the AC-PC (Anterior Commissure - Posterior Commissure) line.
3. The field of view (FOV) must cover the Substantia Nigra (brainstem area).
Figure 11.9: Planning specific slices for Neuromelanin MRI to target the Substantia Nigra in
the midbrain.
11.8
Ultra-Short Echo Time (UTE) Imaging
Conventional MRI sequences utilize minimum echo times (TE) of ∼1–2 milliseconds, resulting
in the T2-Black Hole Problem: tissues whose transverse magnetization decays faster than the
minimum TE (i.e., T2 < 1 ms) are effectively invisible. These ”solid-like” tissues include cortical
bone, tendons, ligaments, and solid-state components like dendrites in non-medical applications.
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p86_c98
content:
Chapter 11. Advanced Imaging Techniques
86
11.8.1
Basic Principle
UTE and ZT E (Zero Echo Time) sequences solve this problem by modifying the RF and gradient
hardware to allow for imaging at echo times as short as 10 microseconds (µs).
• RF Pulse: The RF pulse is transmitted and immediately cut off.
• Acquisition: The data acquisition begins during the RF pulse itself, or immediately
thereafter, circumventing the initial, rapid signal decay of solid components.
Figure 11.10: The Clinical Advantage of Ultra-Short Echo Time (UTE) Imaging in the Knee.
• Image A (Conventional MRI): This image, acquired with a standard Echo Time (TE ≈
5–10 ms), shows the classic T2-Black Hole effect. Tissues with very short T2 (solid-like
collagen structures) are nearly invisible. The signal from the meniscus (red arrows) and
the deep layer of the articular cartilage (yellow arrows) is lost due to rapid signal decay
before image acquisition begins.
• Image B (UTE MRI): This image, acquired with an Ultra-Short Echo Time (TE <
100 µs), successfully captures the signal from the rapidly decaying protons.
The deep
layers of the articular cartilage (yellow arrows) and the fibrotic solid-like components of
the meniscus (red arrows) are clearly visible and appear bright. This capability is essential
for diagnosing early stages of cartilage degeneration and subtle ligament injuries.
11.8.2
Applications of Solid-State MRI
• Musculoskeletal Imaging: UTE allows for the direct visualization of structures pre-
viously invisible to MRI, such as deep collagen structures (meniscus, ligaments) and the
precise integrity of cortical bone.
• Neurosurgery: UTE is critical for imaging the Solid Electrolyte Interphase (SEI)
in certain metal electrodes or the composition of materials used in implants, which have
very short T2 relaxation.
• Non-Medical Imaging: As the external text suggests, Solid-State NMR (a related tech-
nique) is now indispensable for characterizing the chemical and morphological evolution
of lithium-ion battery components, like the formation of dendrites, by providing chemical
information on the Solid Electrolyte Interphases (SEIs).
Fundamentals of MRI

chunk_id: Copy of Mribookv1.3_p87_c99
content:
Chapter 11. Advanced Imaging Techniques
87
11.9
MRI Contrast Agents
Contrast media are often used to improve the visibility of tumors or inflammation. The most
common agents are Gadolinium-based.
Gadolinium is paramagnetic; it does not generate a
signal itself, but it significantly shortens the T1 relaxation time of nearby water protons, making
tissues absorbing the agent appear very bright on T1-weighted images.
Figure 11.11: Effect of Gadolinium contrast agent.
11.9.1
Alternative Contrast Agents
While Gadolinium (Gd3+) is the standard, other agents are sometimes used for specific purposes
based on their magnetic susceptibility:
• Manganese (Mn2+): A paramagnetic agent sometimes used for liver imaging.
• Iron Oxide (Fe2+/Superparamagnetic): Used to darken specific tissues (negative
contrast), particularly for liver and lymph node imaging.
Fundamentals of MRI

1 Before You Begin
About the Product
Performance Characteristics
Advanced Visualization Workspace (AVW) is a software medical device that allows multiple
users to remotely access clinical applications from compatible computers on a network. The
system allows networking, selection, processing, and filming of multimodality DICOM images.
This software is for use with off-the-shelf PC computer technology that meets defined
minimum specifications.
The Advanced Visualization Workspace communicates with imaging systems of different
modalities using the DICOM-3 standard.
Advanced Visualization Workspace Configurations
Advanced Visualization Workspace may be deployed in two configurations:
• Thin Client-Server configuration: This configuration enables widespread remote access via
networked hospital PC’s. The server and client application communicate through a local
area network (LAN) or possibly through the Internet using a VPN connection. The Thin
Client machine has the Graphical User Interface (GUI) and displays images while the central
server retrieves and manages images and generates images for transmission to the client.
Memory and CPU intensive operations such as 3D rendering take place on the server.
Multiple users can login simultaneously and interact with datasets for review and
interpretation. The client software can be deployed on various PCs with different operating
systems and hardware configurations, in accordance with the technical specification
datasheet of the release version.
• Standalone workstation configuration:This configuration supports one (1) user working
locally on the workstation.
Many viewing functions are included in the basic functions, including 2D slice view, thin slab/
MPR view, 3D volumetric images and MIP view. Larger image sets are efficiently and
conveniently reviewed and prepared using the Viewer’s display and manipulation functions.
Basic image manipulation functions include real‐time zooming, scrolling, panning, windowing
and rolling/rotating.
The enterprise server and the client-side systems communicate via TCP/IP network LAN behind
the institution’s firewall. Users may also communicate with the Advanced Visualization
Workspace server computer over the Internet via a Virtual Private Network (VPN) connection
using a broadband connection. The Server runs on Windows Server 2025 (Standard Edition) OS.
Advanced Visualization Workspace client supports the following Microsoft Windows OS
versions:
• Windows 11 (64 bit)
• Windows 10 22H2 (64 bit)

Intended Use/Purpose
The Advanced Visualization Workspace processes clinical images from different modalities and
enables advanced visualization of the images. When used by qualified personnel, it provides
useful diagnostic information. Advanced Visualization Workspace can be used remotely by
multiple users with compatible devices.
Contraindications
This medical device is not to be used for mammography. The device is not intended for
diagnosis of lossy compressed images.
Indications for Use
Philips Advanced Visualization Workspace is a software medical device that allows multiple
users to remotely access clinical applications from compatible computers on a network. The
system allows networking, selection, processing and filming of multimodality DICOM images.
This software is for use with off-the-shelf PC computer technology that meets defined
minimum specifications.
Advanced Visualization Workspace is intended to be used by trained professionals, including
but not limited to physicians and medical technicians.
This medical device is not to be used for mammography.
The device is not intended for diagnosis of lossy compressed images.
• The CT Viewer is an image visualization and post-processing software application designed
to visualize and analyze CT images supporting the physician’s diagnostic process. The
software application supports study review, side-by-side comparison, image fusion, 2D and
3D manipulation, series arrangement, and measurement of CT images.

content:
• The Multimodality Viewer (MMV) is an image visualization and post-processing software
application designed to visualize and analyze multi-modality images in order to assist
clinician's diagnostic process. This software application supports study review, side-by-side
comparison, image fusion, 2D and 3D manipulation, series arrangement, and
measurements of MR, CT, PET, NM, US, DX, CR, RF and XA images. This software application
also supports exporting the processed image series in a dedicated format for assisting
neurosurgical procedures.
• The CT Acute Multi-Functional Review (AMFR) application provides dedicated tools for
findings detection, visualization and assessment of vessels, bones, discs and spine
anatomies, all within a single application.
• The Zero Footprint Viewer (ZFP) is indicated for viewing, sharing, measuring, manipulating
and quantifying of images by referring physicians, clinicians and radiologists, using a web-
browser based viewer with access to hospital network.
ZFP does not create reports and is not intended for diagnosis.
• Multimodality Tumor Tracking (MMTT) is a multi-modality post-processing application used
to display, process, analyze and quantify (in 2D and 3D) anatomical and functional images
for a single study or over the course of multiple time points for CT, Spectral CT, Dual Energy
CT, MR, PET/CT and SPECT/CT. The MMTT application is intended for use on tumors which
are known/confirmed to be pathologically diagnosed cancer. It assists the clinician with the
evaluation, quantification, follow-up and documentation of lesions.
The qEASL (quantitative European Association for the Study of the Liver) is indicated to
assess response after treatment ( i.e. locoregional therapy) on multi-phasic contrast-
enhanced MRI and CT.
• The Multimodality Advanced Vessels Analysis (MM AVA) application is intended to assist
the user in viewing, processing and quantifying vascular conventional or spectral CTA and
MRA datasets of patients with suspected or diagnosed vascular diseases, for the analysis of
vessel anatomy.
• The 3D Modeling application is intended for use as a software interface and image
segmentation application for the transfer of DICOM imaging information to an output file.
The 3D Modeling application output file can be used for fabrication of physical replicas
using additive manufacturing method. The physical replicas can be used for treatment
planning, surgical planning, training and education.
The 3D Modeling application should be used in conjunction with other diagnostic tools and
expert clinical judgment.
• The CT Bone Mineral Analysis (BMA) application supports users with the measurement of
Bone Mineral Density (BMD) in one or multiple time points using an internal (phantom-less)
calibration method on CT imaging.
• The CT Brain Perfusion (BP) application is a post processing software application intended
to assist with the evaluation of an area of interest, to generate qualitative and quantitative
information about changes in image intensity over time. It supports the analysis of
dynamic/serial CT after injection of contrast agent, by calculating the parameters related to
brain perfusion and displays the results as a composite (single image that is calculated from
a set of time course images at a single location) images.

and quantification of blood flow (perfusion), blood volume, time to peak and peak
enhancement using dynamic CT data. The application provides whole-organ or single-
location liver, lung and kidney perfusion calculations.
• CT Calcium Scoring is a post-processing application designed to assist in the quantification
of high-density structures such as calcified lesions in the cardio-thoracic region.
• The CT Cardiac Viewer is indicated for viewing, processing and analysis of cardiac CT
datasets.
• The CT Comprehensive Cardiac Analysis (CCA) application is intended to assist the user in
viewing, processing and quantifying cardiac and coronary CTA datasets of patients with
suspected or diagnosed cardiac disease including coronary artery disease, for the analysis of
heart and coronary artery anatomy and cardiac function.
CT Cardiac Plaque Assessment, an option within the CT CCA application, helps physicians
determine the presence, extent, and properties of coronary plaques.
• CT Pulmo Auto Results is a fully automatic image analysis application that identifies several
radiological findings (e.g. consolidation and ground-glass opacity) to support the
management of adult patients with suspected or diagnosed COVID-19 pneumonia.
• The CT Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) application supports users in viewing
and analysis of Chest CT scans for the assessments of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary
Diseases. The CT COPD application enable localization of affected areas and calculate
diseased lung volume and percentage of affected lungs based on low attenuation areas/
volumes via a guided workflow for airway analysis, reviewing and measuring airway lumen,
and assessing air trapped.
• CT Dental Planning application supports users in processing, viewing, and analyzing dental
CT images. The application allows examination of the patient jaw anatomy and can assist
surgeons in planning oral procedures like implantation of dental implants and jaw surgery.
• The CT Dual Energy Viewer is designed to assist in review and analysis of Dual-Energy CT
Scans and assist in characterization and dual-energy analysis of different tissue materials
based on their energy value.
• CT Liver Analysis is an image processing application and intended for visualization and
analysis of the hepatic CT imaging studies. The application supports users in their workflow
with:
– Automatic classification of the CT contrast phase of each loaded CT series.
– Initial segmentations and 3D visualization of the whole liver, central hepatic and portal
venous branches, central hepatic arterial branches, and spleen.

course of several thoracic studies. Characterizations include diameter, volume, and volume

The CT Spectral Magic Glass on PACS (sMGoP) provides a set of tools to review and analyze

The CT Spectral Light Magic Glass (LMG) option enables the user to review spectral data in a
range of CT applications that are not spectral-enhanced
• The CT TAVI Planning application is intended to be used for patients with aortic valvular
disease, severe symptomatic aortic stenosis or tricuspid aortic valve. The intended part of
the body for this application is the human heart specifically the ascending aorta, aortic root,
coronary ostia and left ventricle in order to assess the aortic valve in pre-operational
planning of transcatheter aortic valve replacement procedures.
CT TAVI Planning is a non-invasive post-processing application providing 3D model-based
segmentation of the aortic valve and aortic arch. The CT TAVI Planning application provides
assessment and measurements of relevant heart structures for TAVI-device sizing, and
allows the user to select a starting angle for C-arm position from the possible optimal
positions from the CT TAVI and select a C-arm angle the user feels is appropriate to use in
the catheterization laboratory by the Interventional team performing the procedure (to be
used during the procedure itself). The physician retains the ultimate responsibility for
making the determination of patient eligibility or which device is implanted based on their
standard practices and additional imaging modalities such as echocardiography
• The CT Multiphase Analysis application creates tissue enhancement maps from multi-phase
conventional or spectral contrast-enhanced CT data.
The application supports the following maps:
– Arterial Enhancement Fraction (AEF): The ratio between the absolute enhancement of
the tissue in the arterial phase and the portal venous phase. The AEF map is intended
for the assessment of liver lesions for oncology patients.

category output representing the estimated quantity of calcium detected together with
preview axial images of the detected calcium meant for informational purposes only. The
device output is available to the radiologist as part of their standard workflow. The CT
Calcium Automated Analysis results are not intended to be used on a stand-alone basis for
risk attribution, clinical decision-making or otherwise preclude clinical assessment of CT
studies.
• The MR Advanced Diffusion Analysis application can be used to perform image viewing,
process and analysis of MRI Diffusion Weighted Images (DWI). The ADA application
supports any oncology and neurology conditions for which diffusion and/or perfusion
analysis are indicated as part of patient management.
• The MR Cardiac Viewer is indicated for side-by-side review of single, multiple or all available
cardiac series in a default or in a user-defined viewing protocol. The MR Cardiac Viewer
supports the user in review of cardiac anatomy and motion.
• MR Cardiac Functional Long Axis: The MR Cardiac Long Axis Functional application is
indicated to assist the user with assessment of LV function from single and multi-slice long
axis cardiac cine data.
• MR Cardiac Functional LV&RV: The MR Cardiac Functional Left Ventricle & Right Ventricle
(LV&RV) application is indicated to support users with assessment of LV and RV function
using multi-slice short axis and axial cardiac MR cine data.
• The MR Cardiac Temporal Enhancement application is indicated to assist users with review
and analysis of individual rest or stress acquisitions and/or rest-stress comparison of multi-
slice dynamic cardiac MR acquisitions in one application.
• The MR Cardiac Spatial Enhancement application allows review, segmentation and
quantification of T1w and T2w multi-slice, single-phase short axis MR images. The
application is indicated to support the user with assessment of myocardial tissue
characteristics that may point to pathologies on the tissue level, such as fibrotic tissue.
• The MR Cardiac Quantitative Mapping application allows to load, review and quantify MR
T1 native, T1 Enhanced, T2 and T2* MR data and to generate parametric maps. The
application is designed to visualize and quantify signal differences for regions of interest
within or between acquisitions. It is indicated to support users with detecting abnormalities
that affect the myocardium in a diffuse fashion, such as edema, fat buildup or storage
diseases.
Indications for Use

content:
• The MR Cardiac Whole Heart application allows users to review cardiac anatomy on 3D or
MRA images and segment the entire heart and surrounding vasculature to create a surface-
rendered 3D model that can be exported for 3D printing. The application is indicated to
assist users with demonstration of anatomical structures for multiple purposes such as
communication with patients, support in planning of ablation procedures or educational
purposes.
• The MR Cartilage Assessment Application is intended to assess the integrity of cartilage on
MRI Data.
• The MR Diffusion application is designed to assist in evaluation of MR Diffusion Weighted
Imaging (DWI) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data to analyze diffusion and anisotropic
properties of tissue. The MR Diffusion Application supports any oncology and neurology
conditions for which diffusion and anisotropic properties of tissue are indicated as part of
patient management.
• MR Image Cumulation is an image processing application enabling the calculation of a result
image based on the accumulation of a selected dimension of an MRI series, such as echo or
b-value. The MR Image Cumulation application supports any condition or anatomy requiring
image enhancement or calculations before image analysis as part of the image
management protocol.
• The MR FiberTrak application supports the user with the viewing, processing and analysis of
Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) data from MR diffusion imaging and with the creation and
visualization of white matter tracks (or diffusional structure) in the brain and spinal tracts.
The MR FiberTrak application supports any related conditions for which tractography
analysis is indicated to assist in therapeutic guidance, clinical decision making, or surgery
preparation for central nervous system cancers, traumatic injuries, and neurological
disorders.
• The MR Brain Function Analysis application assist users in the processing, viewing and
analysis of fMRI Data. The application is designed to support the user to identify and
visualize functional regions of the brain, relying on local metabolic and hemodynamic
changes that occur in activated brain areas.
• MR Liver Health is a post-processing application providing tools to assess anatomical
characteristics and MRI biomarkers (Fat Fraction, T2*/R2*, ADC (Apparent Diffusion
Coefficient) and eADC (exponential ADC)), for the whole liver, its segments, and user-
defined ROIs.
• MR Longitudinal Brain Analysis is a post-processing application to be used for viewing and
evaluating neurological images provided by a magnetic resonance diagnostic device. The
LoBI application is intended for viewing, manipulation, 3D- visualization and comparison of
medical imaging and/or multiple time-points. The LoBI application enables visualization of
information that would otherwise have to be visually compared disjointedly. The LoBI
application provides analysis tools to help the user assess, and document changes in
diagnostic and follow-up examinations. The LoBI application is designed to support the
workflow by helping the user to confirm the absence or presence of lesions, including
evaluation, quantification, follow-up and documentation of any such lesions. The physician
retains the ultimate responsibility for making the final diagnosis and treatment decision.

• The MR Permeability application is designed to visualize T1 Weighted Dynamic Contrast-
Enhanced (DCE) 3D datasets and assist in analyzing the tissue response. The MR
Permeability application supports any related conditions for which permeability analysis is
indicated as part of patient management in the oncology or vascular domain.
• The MR Qflow application supports the visualization and quantification of blood flow
dynamics by assisting in reviewing of MR phase-contrast data.
• MR SpectroView is a task-guided application for the post-processing and visualization of
Proton Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy (MRS) imaging, providing hydrogen single and
multi-voxel spectra, metabolite maps, and/or ratio maps. The MR SpectroView Application
supports the assessment and management of disorders and diseases in the Oncology and
Neurology domain.
• MR Image Algebra is an image processing application enabling basic calculations between
two volumes, such as addition, subtraction, or ratio from a selected dimension of an MRI
series. The MR Image algebra application supports any condition or anatomy requiring
image enhancement or calculations before image analysis as part of the image
management protocol.
• The MR T1 Perfusion post-processing software is indicated to evaluate the Time Intensity
Curves (TIC) of a MR T1 signal enhancement series for patients with oncological lesions
(including brain, prostate, and breast cancer) or inflammatory process (including
musculoskeletal disorders, Crohn's disease).
• MR T2* Neuro Perfusion application is a post processing software application supporting
the analysis of Dynamic Susceptibility Contrast (DSC) T2* perfusion studies to generate
numerical and graphical results of TTP, T0, MTT, rCBV, corrected rCBV, rCBF, Tmax and K2
(leakage). Four methods are available for analysis, including Gamma Variate, Model Free,
Leakage Correction and manual Arterial Input Function (AIF). AIF also enables Perfusion-
Diffusion Mismatch analysis if a Diffusion input dataset is available in addition to the
Perfusion series. The MR T2* Neuro Perfusion application is indicated for the evaluation of
stroke, or assessment and follow-up of brain tumors.
The Diffusion-Perfusion Mismatch in the application is not intended to be used for acute
ischemic stroke patient triage for treatment allocation (e.g., for extended time window for
recanalization therapies according to: Berge, E. et al. (2021) ‘European Stroke Organisation
(ESO) guidelines on intravenous thrombolysis for acute ischaemic stroke’, European Stroke
Journal, 6(1), p. I–LXII. doi:10.1177/2396987321989865, and/or to Powers, W.J. et al. (2018)
2018 Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: A
Guideline for Healthcare Professionals From the American Heart Association/American
Stroke Association, Stroke. doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000158.)

medical professionals, including but not limited to physicians and medical technicians. The main
clinicians or medical and para-medical professionals who use the Philips Advanced Visualization
Workspace are listed below:
• Radiologists in the radiology department/clinic

which are detailed in the individual IFU.

content:
Benefits
When used as specified in the Intended Use, under the circumstances and conditions specified
in the Indications for Use, Advanced Visualization Workspace assists the user with the review
and analysis of clinical image data on par with current - state of the art - clinical practices, thus
realizing a positive impact on diagnosis and patient management.
Undesirable Side Effects
No undesirable side-effects related to the Advanced Visualization Workspace have been
identified.
Measurement Accuracy
The Advanced Visualization Workspace image processing technology is state of the art, and
therefore provides sufficient accuracy to be utilized as a medical device for clinical purpose.
A major factor in determining the accuracy of manual measurements is the ability to accurately
place a measurement control point on an image displayed on a monitor. In addition, the
measurement accuracy is also impacted by the image quality and the user’s interpretation of
the image.
Factors impacting image quality
• Scanner’s calibration and quality control program, including the geometric accuracy,
homogeneity, artifacts, contrast resolution, positioning and sensitometry when applicable.
• Imaging protocol, including spatial resolution (e.g., in-plane resolution, slice thickness),
region of interest, reconstruction algorithm, data corrections (for example scatter), contrast
agent, gating and acquisition sequences when applicable.
• Adherence to patient management and handling procedures, including contrast
administration, scan scheduling, positioning and fixation protocols.
• Pre-existing patient comorbidities
• Residual patient motion and other motion artifacts, such as organ motion.
The following aspects are contributing factors to the user's interpretation of an image
• Image viewing settings (e.g., window setting, zoom)
• Visualization options (e.g., MPR, MIP, or MinIP, volume rendering)
• Extent of the users' knowledge on performing measurements.
• Other relevant factors
Based on their knowledge and experience, clinical users are responsible for:
• Assessing the quality and relevance of the input image interpreting the image for a proper
measurement
• Judging the accuracy of the measurements based on the given image quality

• The "operators" are those persons who actually handle the product.
Before attempting to operate the device, you must read this manual thoroughly, paying
particular attention to all Warnings, Cautions and Notes incorporated in it. You must pay
special attention to all the information given and procedures described in the Safety section.
When you see this symbol, refer to the “Instructions for Use” manual that came

this Instructions for Use and/or any other device.

Notes highlight unusual points as an aid to an operator.

Compatibility
The software product (“AVW“) described in this Instructions for Use communicates with other
products using the DICOM-3 standard (e.g. with imaging systems of different modalities). AVW
uses the DICOM protocol to receive and send lossless images as described in the DICOM
Conformance statement (see Standalone Workstations - DICOM Conformance Statements -
Philips for applicable statement). In addition, AVW uses HL7 through IntelliBridge Enterprise
(IBE) for integration with HIS/RIS systems, to get patients ORM messages and send findings
from clinical applications into a finalized RIS report. Your local Philips representative or
manufacturer can be contacted for any questions regarding compatibility with specific devices
and/or components. Information on significant restrictions related to compatibility can be
found in the Release Notes accompanying this Instructions for Use. Philips is not responsible for
running compatibility validation of non-supported third-party software.
In case of off the shelf hardware (server/workstation) provided by Philips Health Systems
personnel or a virtual machine provided by the hospital according to Philips defined
specifications:
Changes and/or additions to the server/workstation should only be carried out by Philips Health
Systems or by third parties expressly authorized by Philips Health Systems to do so.
Any addition or change to software products installed on the server/workstation or changes of
operating system configuration is restricted, unless the other software equipment or
components are recognized as compatible by Philips. A list of such software, equipment and
components is available on request from your local Philips Representative, or the
Manufacturer. Philips is not responsible for running compatibility validation of non-supported
third-party software.
Any changes and/or additions must comply with all applicable laws and regulations that have
the force of law within the jurisdiction(s) concerned, and with best engineering practice.
Changes and/or additions carried out by persons without the appropriate training, and/or using
unapproved spare parts, may lead to the Philips Health Systems warranty being voided. Philips
is not responsible for any malfunction of AVW, if AVW runs on hardware that is not according
to hardware specifications. If not supplied by Philips with the AVW software, Philips is not
responsible for any malfunction of the hardware used. As with all complex technical equipment,
maintenance by persons not appropriately qualified and/or using unapproved spare parts
carries serious risks of damage to the equipment and of personal injury.
Compliance
The Advanced Visualization Workspace complies with relevant international and national
standards and laws. Information on compliance is supplied on request by your local Philips
representative, or by Manufacturer.
This software product shall be installed on appropriate IT equipment that complies with
relevant international and national laws and standards on EMC (Electro-Magnetic
Compatibility) and Electrical Safety. Such laws and standards define both the permissible
electromagnetic emission levels from equipment and its required immunity to electromagnetic
interference from external sources.

Network Safety, Security, and Privacy
Philips recognizes that the security of Philips products is an important part of your facility's
security-in-depth strategy. However, protection can only be realized if you implement a
comprehensive, multi-layered strategy (including policies, processes, and technologies) to
protect information and systems from internal and external threats.
Following industry-standard practice, your strategy should address:
• Physical security;
• Operational security;
• Procedural security;
• Risk management;
• Security policies; and
• Contingency planning.
The practical implementation of technical security elements varies by site and may employ a
number of technologies, including firewalls, virus-scanning software, authentication
technologies, etc.
As with any computer-based system, protection must be provided so that firewalls and/or
other security devices are in place between the medical system and any externally accessible
systems. The USA Veterans Administration has developed a widely used Medical Device
Isolation Architecture for this purpose. Such perimeter and network defenses are essential
elements in a comprehensive medical device security strategy.
Any device connection to an internal or external network should be done with appropriate risk
management for product effectiveness and data and systems security. Additional security and
privacy information can be found on the Philips product security website at:
www.philips.com/productsecurity
Please review Philips product security policies regarding remote service, patch management,
anti-virus software and more in the “Product Security Policy Statement” and additional
information sources available through this website.
NOTICE
Philips is not responsible for security of hospital managed systems (desktop PCs, laptops)
where the Advanced Visualization Workspace client is installed.

Security Issues and Guidelines
In addition to the patient information and device integrity needs discussed in the preceding
section on regulatory requirements, the following topics, issues, and guidelines should be
understood and addressed by operators and owners.
This applies Philips Advanced Visualization Workspace and Console and not the client PCs
Security events can be monitored and addressed through:
• A Philips-authorized service organization, using approved service tools and procedures,
and/or
• The hospital’s IT solutions for security monitoring (e.g., SIEM, network monitoring systems),
depending on the customer’s deployment model.
The solution includes built-in antivirus protection that continuously monitors for malicious
software. If a virus or malware threat is detected, the system provides an immediate indication
to alert the user and/or system administrator.
The solution enables logging of all relevant security events, including but not limited to
malware detection, unauthorized access attempts, configuration changes, and network
anomalies. Audit logs and security-relevant information are protected against unauthorized
modification and are accessible only to authorized personnel.
These capabilities support timely incident detection, investigation, and response while
maintaining the safety and intended clinical functionality of the device.
If you suspect a cybersecurity incident, including unauthorized access, malware infection,
unusual device behavior, or other security concerns, contact your local Philips representatives
or visit Philips security information | Philips.
Network Security
The Philips Advanced Visualization Workspace must be placed on a secure local computer
network that has protections against viruses and other harmful computer system intruders.
Make sure the equipment is connected to a local network that uses appropriate protection,
such as a firewall and virus scanners.
CAUTION
The Advanced Visualization Workspace system does not require open Internet connectivity
for its standard Intended Use. It is strongly recommended that the Advanced Visualization
Workspace Server/Workstation not be used for Internet browsing to prevent exposure to
the public internet.
Remote Service
Remote Service provides a set of tools that enable Philips to perform monitoring and service
actions, entirely or partly, from a remote location. Remote Service is designed to reduce system
downtime and improve investigation of systemic issues.

Positioning of Display Monitors
Unauthorized visual access to protected information can be minimized by positioning the
system’s display monitor so it faces a wall, to prevent viewing from doorways, hallways and
other traffic areas.
NOTICE
Monitor position is a suggestion for use with monitors of the Advanced Visualization
Workspace Client PCs and the Advanced Visualization Workspace Workstation.
To help in limiting unauthorized visual access, an unattended computer display automatically
goes blank after a set period of time.
The Advanced Visualization Workspace system supports Automatic Logoff/Screen Lock. For
additional information, see “Automatic Logoff (Lock Screen)” on page 41.
Room Access Control
Procedures must be put in place to limit physical access to the medical device, to prevent
accidental, casual or deliberate contact by unauthorized individuals.
Access to the room containing the Advanced Visualization Workspace server or workstation
should be controlled by policy and procedures that identify who is authorized to occupy specific
areas. Check with your hospital’s Safety and Security Office for more information on what
measures are in place or how to implement room access controls.
User Login and Logout Protections
A consistent user login process (user names and passwords) provides good security of
protected information. Minimum login standards include:
• Implementing strong passwords. This is the easiest and most effective method to increase
security. Strong passwords consist of at least eight alphanumeric, mixed case characters,
digits and special characters like '@' or '*'.
• Never use words that can be found in the dictionary.
• Never post or share user names and passwords.
• Change passwords periodically.

Additional Security and Privacy Features
HIPAA defines a number of physical and technical safeguards which are either required or
addressable. Some features that could implement these functions are different or not
implemented for reasons mentioned below. This section also lists other information related to
security features that are not implemented and that the owner of the systems should be aware
of.
Backup Procedure
The system is not intended for permanently storing sensitive patient personal information.
Information should be exported to a long-term storage device as soon as possible.
Emergency Access Procedure
The Advanced Visualization Workspace system does not have a built-in emergency user
account. However, it supports the creation of unique user accounts and assignment of
permissions to users. Hospital administrators can use this function to create an “emergency”
user account with the necessary permissions. To avoid unauthorized access to patient data,
ensure that knowledge of this generic “emergency” user account and access to the system is
restricted.
The Advanced Visualization Workspace system does not allow or enforce generic account users
to enter their real names, which restricts the system’s ability to track and audit the generic user
account.
It is not possible to clearly mark data output (e.g., screen, print-out and exported data to DVD)
as having been created during an emergency access operation.
Encryption
Windows BitLocker, a full disk encryption feature (provided by the Windows OS) that protects
data by encrypting entire volumes, can be enabled by the Hospital Administrator as needed, to
encrypt data at rest on the Advanced Visualization Workspace server.
For data in transit, the Advanced Visualization Workspace system supports the IHEATNA profile,
which enables secure transmission of ePHI between configured DICOM devices.
Physical Access to System
The Advanced Visualization Workspace system should be placed in an access restricted area in
the hospital. However, the following characteristics are to be taken into account for system
operation and access control:
• The computer case is "service friendly" (e.g., accessing and removing the hard drive does
not require tools). However, the computer case can be locked (e.g., by cable lock).
• The boot order for the system is DVD, USB, hard disk. By inserting bootable CD/DVD or
connecting bootable USB memory device, the system may start up from those and thus
